Computer science

 Home
OurBigBook.com Words: 64k Articles: 875
Computer science studies how information can be represented and transformed by algorithms, and what those transformations can achieve. Its central questions connect mathematics to practical design: what answer should a procedure produce, why is it correct, and how much work does it require as its input grows? Computability theory asks which tasks can be solved at all; computational complexity theory asks what resources a solution needs.
The beauty is that choosing a representation can change what is feasible. Finding a name among a million entries sounds like a million checks. Store the entries in a sorted array, and binary search needs at most twenty middle-entry comparisons. The order makes each unsuccessful comparison eliminate a whole region of possibilities. A data structure supplies useful organization; an algorithm exploits it; time complexity explains the resulting savings.
Algorithm correctness covers every permitted input, including absent names and empty collections. Time complexity predicts scaling; statistical program profiling investigates a particular implementation.

Raster graphics

Words: 1k Articles: 4
Computer graphics OurBigBook.com
Raster graphics describe a picture by an array of pixels on a grid. For a rectangular image of width W and height H, write its stored values as prc​, with 0≤r<H and 0≤c<W. A grayscale pixel can have one shade value; a colour pixel can have several component values. The grid specifies where values belong, while the encoding specifies what those values mean. A raster image therefore needs dimensions and an interpretation of its samples, not just a string of numbers.
The appealing feature is that pictures become explicit data: selecting a rectangle selects entries of an array; comparing two images compares their pixel values; image compression can exploit repeated or related values. Raster sampling and reconstruction explains why the stored grid and the displayed picture are different objects. A square drawn around a sample is one display convention, not a claim that the original scene consisted of little squares.
For example, a 6×4 grayscale raster image stores 24 pixel values, even when displayed across a much larger rectangle. With one unsigned eight-bit sample per pixel, its uncompressed sample payload is 24⋅8=192 bits; a file format can additionally require a file header, padding and other information, and image compression can change the stored size.
Enlarging that image can copy each pixel into a block through nearest-neighbor interpolation, or infer intermediate values through interpolation. Either procedure supplies a reconstruction rule; neither determines which unrecorded detail was present in the original. Vector graphics use a different representation, specifying geometric objects to be rendered onto a chosen grid. Re-rendering such a description and enlarging an existing raster image are different operations.

Pixel

Words: 350 Articles: 1
Raster graphics OurBigBook.com
A pixel is one picture element at an indexed position in a raster image. It can contain a single grayscale value or several colour components. The word can also refer to a physical display element; the indexed element of the stored image is the meaning used here. One stored pixel need not occupy exactly one physical display element when the image is resized. Microsoft's bitmap documentation likewise distinguishes an image's grid and its numerical colour representation.[ref]
Separate position from value: raster sampling and reconstruction concerns the spatial grid, while sample depth concerns how many bits encode each component. Four times as many pixels can describe a finer grid without improving the quantization of any value. Conversely, more bits per sample can distinguish more shades without locating an edge more precisely.
In the binary example under run-length encoding, one bit per pixel selects black or white. In the grayscale example under lossy block averaging, eight bits per pixel select one of 256 codes. Calling them codes keeps their numerical values distinct from the physical light that a display emits.
Sample depth (b,2b)
Words: 184
Pixel OurBigBook.com
The sample depth b is the number of bits allocated to one stored sample. An unsigned b-bit integer has 2b codes, 0,…,2b−1. This is per component, not automatically per pixel: three eight-bit components require 24 payload bits per pixel. A raster image with WH pixels and k such components requires WHkb payload bits before data compression, padding or a file header.
For a toy normalized shade x∈[0,1], define uniform quantization with endpoints included by
qb​(x)=⌊(2b−1)x+21​⌋,xb​=2b−1qb​(x)​.
(1)
The floor function implements rounding to the nearest code, with exact halves rounded upward. The reconstruction step is δb​=1/(2b−1), and ∣xb​−x∣≤δb​/2. For b=2, the levels are 0,1/3,2/3,1; for b=8 they are 0,1/255,…,1. Increasing sample depth refines this value grid without changing the spatial grid. These levels are uniform in x; if x is encoded sRGB, they are not uniform in relative luminance.
PNG uses a bit-depth field per sample or palette index. Its grayscale type without alpha permits 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 bits per sample; its truecolour type permits 8 or 16 bits per component. These are format-specific restrictions, not a rule for every raster image.[ref]

Grayscale

Words: 300
Raster graphics OurBigBook.com
A grayscale image varies along shades from black to white rather than recording independent colour differences. A numerical grayscale image assigns one shade sample to each pixel; an encoding determines how that sample maps to a displayed shade. A colour raster image can also look grayscale, for example when its three sRGB components are equal.
The convention in our lossy block averaging example is black at the integer code 0 and white at 255. Its arithmetic means act on those stored codes. This is a fully specified numerical experiment, but it does not claim that code 128 means half the physical light of code 255. PNG explicitly allows samples that are not proportional to light: its grayscale interpretation depends on the indicated transfer curve, and can be device-dependent when that information is absent.[ref]
Two different questions therefore need different operations. To average stored codes, average the integers. To average relative luminance for neutral sRGB shades, decode the codes to linear light, average there, and encode the result again. Equal weights on black and white give encoded value 1/2 by the first method, but approximately 0.73536 by the second. Rounded to eight-bit codes these are 128 and 188. This example concerns ideal neutral shades and the specified sRGB conversion; it does not assert a universal grayscale conversion for every colour encoding.
The upper panels hold the spatial grid fixed and change sample depth: four levels produce broad constant bands, while 256 levels make smaller numerical steps. The lower panels hold the colour interpretation fixed and compare encoded sRGB values with relative luminance. All panels are calculated synthetic examples, not measured display data. Grayscale is useful when shade structure is the quantity of interest: a synthetic scalar image signal can be inspected without introducing separate colour components.

Raster sampling and reconstruction (prc​=f(xc​,yr​))

Words: 371
Raster graphics OurBigBook.com
A point-sampling model assigns prc​=f(xc​,yr​) to a pixel on a grid, where f is a continuous function representing an image signal. An area-sampling model instead assigns the average value of a function over a specified footprint. These are different models: a narrow feature between point samples can be missed, whereas its contribution to an area sample depends on its width and shade. Neither model says that the recorded value uniquely determines everything inside a grid cell.
The upper panels start with exactly the same 6×4 array. Nearest-neighbor interpolation repeats its values into a 24×16 display; successive linear interpolations in the two coordinate directions produce a smoother 24×16 display. Original sample positions are marked. Both displays use 384 output pixels, but only the same 24 recorded values. The extra values follow the chosen interpolation rule. Between-grid appearance is inferred, not independently recorded.
Spatial resolution needs a stated meaning. A grid over a rectangle of width Lx​ and height Ly​ has nominal cell pitches Δx=Lx​/W and Δy=Ly​/H. Over the same rectangle, doubling both dimensions halves these pitches and quadruples the pixel count. That is a finer grid, not a guarantee of more recoverable detail. Blurring before sampling, quantization and aliasing can make different originals share the same recorded array. Enlarging the rectangle without adding samples instead increases the displayed pitch.
A reproducible computational demonstration makes the ambiguity exact. Take the one-dimensional profiles f(x)=0.5+0.4sin(2πx) and g(x)=0.5+0.4sin(10πx), repeated identically along every row. Sample at xj​=j/4 for j=0,…,8. Since 10πxj​=2πxj​+2πj, the fact that the sine is a periodic function gives f(xj​)=g(xj​). Both yield 0.5,0.9,0.5,0.1,0.5,0.9,0.5,0.1,0.5, although at x=1/8 they give approximately 0.78284 and 0.21716. The lower panel draws both originals and their common samples: no operation on those samples alone can identify the original profile. This is aliasing in an ideal point-sampling model, without image noise or rounding.
The Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem describes reconstruction under a bandwidth restriction and ideal sampling assumptions; it does not grant uniqueness for arbitrary image signals from a finite raster image.[ref] The beautiful lesson is constructive: choose what detail the grid should preserve before sampling, and choose a reconstruction rule suited to the information actually retained.

sRGB

Words: 270 Articles: 1
Computer graphics OurBigBook.com
sRGB specifies a red-green-blue colour encoding. Restricting attention to component values in [0,1], its encoded component s corresponds to the linear-light component
D(s)={s/12.92,((s+0.055)/1.055)2.4,​0≤s≤0.04045,0.04045<s≤1.​
(2)
Thus the conversion is piecewise, not a single power law. The reverse conversion used here is
E(l)={12.92l,1.055l1/2.4−0.055,​0≤l≤0.0031308,0.0031308<l≤1.​
(3)
These conventional rounded thresholds are used by the W3C conversion routines; they give a tiny mismatch at the join rather than a mathematically exact pair of inverses everywhere.[ref][ref]
For an eight-bit neutral grayscale code q, use s=q/255 in all three components. Its relative luminance is then D(s). For example, D(0.5)≈0.21404, whereas E(0.5)≈0.73536. This is why averaging encoded values and averaging linear light give different answers. sRGB is a specified interpretation; merely calling a raster image grayscale does not imply it uses sRGB.

Relative luminance (Y)

Words: 125
sRGB OurBigBook.com
For the normalized sRGB calculations here, relative luminance is the linear-light weighted sum
Y=0.2126R+0.7152G+0.0722B,
(4)
where R,G,B are decoded linear-light components, not encoded code values. This is the sRGB calculation specified in W3C's WCAG 2.2 definition of relative luminance. It places reference black at 0 and reference white at 1; it does not by itself specify an absolute display light level.[ref]
For a neutral sRGB shade, R=G=B=l, and the weights sum to 1, so Y=l. For a coloured pixel, relative luminance can be encoded as a neutral sRGB shade with all three encoded components E(Y). This preserves the specified Y while discarding colour differences; it is one precisely defined grayscale conversion, not a unique way to turn all colour images into grayscale.

Vector graphics

Words: 1k Articles: 1
Computer graphics OurBigBook.com
Vector graphics represent a picture by geometric objects and instructions for drawing them: positions, shapes, fills, boundary strokes and transformations. A circle can be stored as a centre and radius; a rectangle as a corner, width and height; a polygon as an ordered list of vertices. These geometric primitives describe whole objects rather than assigning a colour to every pixel. SVG provides elements for such basic shapes and for paths assembled from line segments and curves.[ref]
The useful separation is between the stored geometry and the finite output. A circle of radius 2 remains the same geometric description whether rendered across twenty or two thousand output pixels. This is the sense in which vector graphics are resolution independent: increasing the output grid can evaluate the original geometry again. The resulting raster image still has finite spatial resolution, and numerical coordinates have finite precision. Enlarging a previously rendered raster image through interpolation instead works with its existing samples. Neither operation guarantees that arbitrarily thin details remain visible at every size.
An SVG path uses a current point and drawing commands. For example, M 1 4 L 5 4 L 3 1 Z moves to (1,4), draws two line segments, then closes back to the starting point, giving a triangle. Uppercase commands use absolute coordinates; the corresponding lowercase commands use offsets from the current point. Thus M 1 4 l 4 0 l -2 -3 z describes the same triangle. The coordinates belong to the current user Cartesian coordinate system, not necessarily to output pixels.[ref]
For a curved example, the path M 1 4 Q 3 0 5 4 Z uses one quadratic Bézier curve followed by a closing line segment. With control points P0​=(1,4), P1​=(3,0) and P2​=(5,4), its curved boundary is
B(t)=(1−t)2P0​+2t(1−t)P1​+t2P2​=(1+4t,4−8t+8t2),0≤t≤1.
(5)
The endpoints are P0​,P2​, and B(1/2)=(3,2); the interior control point P1​ is not a point on the curve. A fill paints the enclosed region, while a stroke paints a band around its boundary with a chosen width. One can use either or both: geometry and paint instructions are distinct.[ref][ref]
The first illustration uses increasing y downward, following the initial SVG coordinate convention. Its dashed control polygon guides the eye; it is not part of the filled path. Apply the affine map
T(x,y)=(1.5x+0.5y+1,y+1),A=(1.50​0.51​).
(6)
This combines horizontal scaling, a shear mapping and a translation. The transformed control points are (4.5,5), (5.5,1) and (10.5,5), giving the path M 4.5 5 Q 5.5 1 10.5 5 Z. Its curved midpoint is T(3,2)=(6.5,3). The affine equivariance of a geometric basis explains why transforming only the control points transforms the entire Bézier curve: its weights sum to one, so the translation is added exactly once. The enclosed area is ∫01​8t(1−t)⋅4dt=16/3 before transformation and ∣detA∣⋅16/3=8 afterwards. These checks concern the filled region, excluding the width of any stroke.
An SVG viewBox specifies a rectangle in user coordinates to map into a display region. For example, viewBox="0 0 6 6" in a square viewport of 120 by 120 display units gives a scale of 20 display units per user unit; in a square viewport of 600 by 600 it gives 100. The path's control points need not change. For unequal proportions, preserveAspectRatio controls whether the mapping preserves proportions or stretches the axes separately. These display units need not correspond one for one to physical display pixels.[ref][ref]
Rasterization converts the geometric drawing into a raster image on a chosen grid. Deciding whether each pixel centre lies inside a filled region is a simple rule, but a moving diagonal boundary can make entire pixels switch abruptly. Antialiasing reduces these sampling artifacts by accounting for a footprint around each sample, rather than treating every pixel as a single inside-or-outside decision. This connects vector graphics to raster sampling and reconstruction and aliasing; a finer grid and a better sampling rule solve different parts of the problem.
For an exact analytical model, fill the region R={(x,y)∈[0,4]2:y≤x+1/4}. For a square pixel footprint S, let
αS​=area(S)area(R∩S)​,LS​=αS​Lfill​+(1−αS​)Lbackground​.
(7)
Here αS​ is geometric coverage, and L is relative luminance for ideal opaque neutral shades, with Lfill​=0 and Lbackground​=1. The intersection and area determine how much of the footprint is covered. This is a specified area-average model, not a claim that every SVG renderer uses exact coverage. The SVG shape-rendering property supplies rendering hints and permits implementation tradeoffs, including disabling antialiasing for some choices.[ref]
On the 4×4 grid of unit squares, S=[0,1]×[0,1] has coverage αS​=1−(3/4)2/2=23/32, whereas the pixel centre (1/2,1/2) lies inside R and gives coverage 1 under the centre rule. The adjacent square [0,1]×[1,2] has coverage 1/32 but its centre lies outside. The entire filled area is 16−(15/4)2/2=287/32. Summing exact coverage times cell area gives this value on both the 4×4 and 16×16 grids; the coarse centre rule instead gives 10. Coverage values are displayed after sRGB encoding of the modeled relative luminance. The thin coloured line is a geometry overlay, not an extra sampled stroke. Enlarging the middle panel by nearest-neighbor interpolation would repeat its sixteen values; re-rendering the geometry produces the 256 independently evaluated footprints in the right panel. Antialiasing reduces abrupt edges but cannot make a finite grid preserve every geometric detail.
The attractive feature of vector graphics is editability at the level of intent: move one control point to bend a boundary, change a circle's radius, or transform a whole diagram while keeping its parts aligned. Logos, technical diagrams and outline fonts benefit because their structure can be expressed with relatively few shapes and curves. A complicated photograph may require enormous geometric detail, so vector graphics do not imply a smaller file than raster graphics. Nor does an SVG container guarantee that every object is vector geometry: its image element can embed or reference a PNG raster image. Transforming that embedded raster image changes its placement and reconstruction, but does not recover missing original detail.[ref]

SVG

Words: 65
Vector graphics OurBigBook.com
SVG, short for Scalable Vector Graphics, is a markup file format for two-dimensional graphics, specified by the W3C SVG Working Group. It describes vector graphics shapes, text and image objects, with grouping and transformations; it can therefore contain both geometric objects and raster images. The small command strings in vector graphics are path data within this format, not complete standalone documents.[ref]

File format

Words: 55 Articles: 1
Computer science OurBigBook.com
A file format specifies how a binary string is interpreted: field order, field widths, permitted values and where decoding stops. A data compression comparison must include all fields required to recover the data.

File header

Words: 28
File format OurBigBook.com
A file header is leading information describing how to interpret the following data. Dimensions and a choice of compression method are examples. The two toy image compression examples explicitly count these fields.

Data compression

Words: 3k Articles: 13
Computer science OurBigBook.com
Data compression represents data using fewer bits than a specified original representation. The saving can reduce storage in a file system and reduce the number of bits sent through a communication channel. At a fixed transmission rate, fewer bits arrive sooner; this makes better use of a fixed transmission budget. Both the encoded data and the instructions needed to interpret them contribute to the size of a stored file.
There are two different promises. Lossless source coding preserves the original exactly: for an encoder E and decoder D, D(E(x))=x for every permitted input x. Thus E must be an injective function. Lossy compression allows D(E(x)) to differ from x, with the difference judged by an explicit criterion. A program or numerical record may require exact recovery; a preview image may tolerate altered pixels in return for fewer bits.
The appeal of lossless source coding is that repetition can be described rather than copied. Run-length encoding says "repeat this value twelve times"; a prefix code can give more frequent symbols shorter descriptions. These are distinct ways to exploit structure, and neither promises savings for every input. Image compression supplies especially visible examples of both lossless source coding and lossy compression.
Claude E. Shannon's 1948 paper made the role of probability distributions precise. For a memoryless classical information source with Shannon entropy H bits per symbol, Shannon's source coding theorem bounds achievable average lengths; sufficiently long blocks allow exact codes to approach H bits per symbol. This is a statement about a specified source and average lengths, not a promise to shorten every message.[ref]

Universal lossless shortening is impossible

Words: 129
Data compression OurBigBook.com
Fix n≥1. There is no injective function from all length-n binary strings to binary strings of length strictly less than n. There are 2n possible inputs, but even allowing the empty string gives only
∑k=0n−1​2k=2n−1
(8)
possible shorter outputs. The finite geometric series and pigeonhole principle leave at least two inputs sharing an output, which prevents exact decoding. For n=3, eight inputs compete for the empty string and the six strings 0, 1, 00, 01, 10, 11.
This counting argument includes any file header or other information sent to the decoder. An algorithm chosen separately for each input must also be identified to the receiver; its description is not free. A useful compressor saves space on some inputs while leaving others unchanged or making them longer. Lossy compression avoids the exact-recovery requirement by deliberately allowing several inputs to share an output.

Lossy compression

Words: 532 Articles: 1
Data compression OurBigBook.com
Lossy compression reduces a representation while permitting irreversible changes to the original. The encoder can map distinct inputs to the same output, so its decoder cannot recover both originals exactly. The useful question becomes how much storage is saved for an acceptable amount of distortion: mean squared error is one numerical criterion, but it does not by itself measure how noticeable a visual change is.
For example, storing the arithmetic mean of four grayscale pixels retains their average shade while discarding their arrangement. Blocks (0100​1000​) and (5050​5050​) both produce 50. The former has detail and the latter is uniform, yet the decoder receives the same value. Lossy block averaging makes this ambiguity, its bit saving and its mean squared error exact.

Lossy block averaging (qij​=⌊mij​+1/2⌋)

Words: 428
Lossy compression OurBigBook.com
This toy image compression method stores one rounded arithmetic mean for each disjoint 2×2 block of grayscale pixels. The quantization rule is round to the nearest integer, with exact halves rounded upward. Each stored value is an unsigned eight-bit integer. Reconstruction fills the original block with that value, a form of nearest-neighbor interpolation. Averaging already discards information; rounding can discard more.
Here is an exact 16×16 source array. Index rows and columns by r,c∈{0,…,15} and define
brc​xrc​​=40+10⌊r/2⌋+12⌊c/2⌋,=brc​+20(−1)r+c+1{r even, c even}​.​
(9)
The floor function makes b constant within each block; the indicator function adds 1 only to its upper-left pixel. All values are integers from 20 to 215. Each block therefore has the exact form
(b+21b−20​b−20b+20​),m=b+41​,q=⌊m+21​⌋=b.
(10)
For example, the upper-left block (6120​2060​) has arithmetic mean 161/4=40.25 and is stored as 40. The block immediately to its right (7332​3272​) is stored as 52. The complete stored 8×8 array is specified by qij​=40+10i+12j for 0≤i,j≤7. Its first row is 40,52,64,76,88,100,112,124; its last is 110,122,134,146,158,170,182,194.
This toy file format again has eight-bit width and height fields followed by a one-bit mode: 0 means raw eight-bit grayscale pixels, 1 means the rounded block arithmetic means. This profile accepts only width and height 16. The decoder knows the block size and reconstruction rule from the format, reads the 64 stored values in row order, and repeats each across its corresponding 2×2 block. The original 256 pixels cost 256⋅8=2048 payload bits; the 64 stored values cost 64⋅8=512 payload bits. The reduction is 75%. These payload counts exclude the common 17-bit file header; complete sizes are 2065 and 529 bits, or 2072 and 536 bits after final zero padding to eight-bit units. There is no stored codebook or additional prediction rule.
The empirical mean squared error averages squared differences over the 256 original pixel positions:
MSE=2561​∑r=015​∑c=015​(xrc​−xrc​)2=4212+202+202+202​=410.25.
(11)
Every block has the same four errors, so this value is exact in squared stored shade units. If the unrounded arithmetic mean b+1/4 could be reconstructed, the error would instead be 410.1875; eight-bit quantization adds 0.0625. That hypothetical comparison does not count fractional means as free eight-bit values.
The broad shade pattern survives, while the alternating bright and dark pixels vanish. Indeed, a second source with every block constant at b produces the identical stored array q: exact decoding of both sources is impossible. This makes the storage benefit and the lost detail visible at once. Block averaging is useful for a coarse preview when the individual pixels are dispensable; choosing an acceptable mean squared error or visual result is part of the application, not a guarantee supplied by the encoder.

Run-length encoding

Words: 515
Data compression OurBigBook.com
Run-length encoding replaces each maximal consecutive group of equal values, called a run, by its value and length. Decoding repeats each value the specified number of times. It is lossless source coding: no values are discarded. For a binary string, successive maximal runs alternate between 0 and 1, so storing the first bit and all run lengths is enough.
Take this 8×8 raster image, with 0 black and 1 white, read left to right across each row and then top to bottom:
00000000
00001111
11110000
00001111
11110000
00001111
11110000
00000000
Reading the whole image as one 64-bit binary string gives exactly seven runs:
(value,length)=(0,12),(1,8),(0,8),(1,8),(0,8),(1,8),(0,12).
(12)
The lengths sum to 12+8+8+8+8+8+12=64. Repeating the alternating values for these lengths and splitting after every eighth pixel reconstructs every displayed row exactly.
Here is a complete toy file format. Its file header is an eight-bit unsigned width, an eight-bit unsigned height, then a one-bit mode: 0 means raw pixels, 1 means run-length encoding. Fields are written most significant bit first; this profile accepts only width and height 8, so both decoders know to stop at 64 pixels. Raw mode contains 64 bits. RLE mode contains the initial bit, followed by seven-bit unsigned run lengths in the range 1 to 64. Zero and lengths above 64 are invalid; a decoder rejects a run that would exceed the remaining pixel count. It stops when the decoded lengths sum to 64, so no run-count field or end marker is needed.
For this image, the complete RLE serialization is:
00001000 00001000 1 | 0 | 0001100 0001000 0001000 0001000 0001000 0001000 0001100
Spaces and vertical bars are explanatory separators, not stored characters. The seven-bit fields directly store the lengths; 64 would be 1000000. The payload costs 1+7⋅7=50 bits, versus 64 raw bits. The 17-bit file header has the same size in either mode, giving complete sizes of 67 versus 81 bits. If packed into eight-bit units, append zero padding only at the end: the sizes become 72 versus 88 bits. These are sizes of this toy representation, not sizes of PNG files.
The field design matters. Restarting RLE on every row costs eight initial bits plus four bits per run when lengths are stored directly: three bits represent only 0 through 7, whereas a row can have length 8. This pattern has row-run counts 1,2,2,2,2,2,2,1, totalling 14, so that payload costs 8+4⋅14=64 bits, with no saving. Storing length minus one would instead fit lengths 1 through 8 into three bits, but is a different declared file format. An alternating flat 64-bit binary string has 64 runs and costs 1+7⋅64=449 payload bits in our flat format; restarting each row costs 8+4⋅64=264 payload bits. A one-run image costs only eight payload bits. These extremes explain when RLE is useful: long uninterrupted regions make short instructions, while frequent changes make instructions expensive.
Prefix codes of unequal lengths can replace fixed-width run lengths, provided the decoder knows the code and any necessary code description is counted. Run-length encoding names a technique, not one universal serialization. For a real implementation, Microsoft's bitmap documentation specifies BI_RLE8 with count and value fields plus special commands, rather than our initial-bit convention.[ref]

Deflate

Words: 1k Articles: 6
Data compression OurBigBook.com
Deflate is the lossless source coding method specified for PNG compression. It can describe repeated stretches of earlier data, going beyond the single-value repetitions of run-length encoding.[ref]
The format combines Deflate backreferences, which describe repeated stretches, with Deflate Huffman coding, which represents the resulting instructions using prefix codes. Deflate block framing tells the decoder which codes apply and where decoding stops. RFC 1951, DEFLATE Compressed Data Format Specification version 1.3 (May 1996), defines the format; different encoders can choose different instructions for the same input.[ref]
This separation is useful: discovering a repeated phrase and choosing short codewords solve different problems. A repeated phrase can contain many distinct bytes, while unequal codeword lengths can help even when no phrase repeats. Neither mechanism removes Deflate compression overhead or guarantees a saving on every input.

Deflate literal byte

Words: 46
Deflate OurBigBook.com
A Deflate literal byte instructs the decoder to append one specified byte directly to the output. For example, three Deflate literal bytes with values 65, 66 and 67 produce ABC. These values are symbols in the Deflate Huffman coding stage, rather than necessarily eight raw stored bits each. A Deflate backreference instead describes a copy from earlier output.

Deflate backreference ((ℓ,d))

Words: 351 Articles: 1
Deflate OurBigBook.com
A Deflate backreference specifies a length ℓ and backward distance d, measured in decoded bytes. If n bytes have already been produced, append ℓ bytes starting at output index n−d, counting indices from zero. The permitted ranges are 3≤ℓ≤258 and 1≤d≤32768. Without a supplied initial history, d≤n is also required. The distance refers to decoded history, not a position in the compressed input.[ref]
For the twelve bytes ABCABCABCABC, an illustrative instruction sequence is three Deflate literal bytes A, B, C, followed by the Deflate backreference (ℓ,d)=(9,3). Run-length encoding sees twelve single-byte runs because neighbouring values differ; the Deflate backreference describes a repeated three-byte pattern instead. Conversely, a Deflate literal byte A followed by (7,1) produces AAAAAAAA: distance one can express a single-value repetition. These are chosen instructional examples, not claims about an encoder's chosen instructions or complete serialized streams.
Deflate overlapping copy
Words: 206
Deflate backreference OurBigBook.com
In a Deflate overlapping copy, ℓ>d: some source bytes are created by the very copy being decoded. For each step i=0,…,ℓ−1, read the current output at index n+i−d and append that byte at index n+i. Because d≥1, the source index is always smaller than the destination index, so the needed byte exists when it is read.[ref]
For ABC followed by (9,3), the source indices are 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8 and the destination indices are 3,4,5,6,7,8,9,10,11. Steps 0 through 2 copy the original ABC; steps 3 through 5 copy the ABC just appended; steps 6 through 8 copy the next newly appended ABC. Thus the final output is exactly ABCABCABCABC. Taking a snapshot of the original three-byte source slice would produce only three bytes; that operation does not implement the specified nine-byte copy.
The reusable idea is a short description of periodic continuation: the decoder repeatedly looks a fixed distance behind its growing output. A Deflate backreference can also reach across a Deflate block framing boundary. Changing the block's Huffman codes does not by itself erase the decoded history.[ref]

Deflate Huffman coding

Words: 235
Deflate OurBigBook.com
For a compressed block, Deflate Huffman coding uses one alphabet for Deflate literal bytes, length symbols and the end-of-block symbol, and another alphabet for distance symbols. Values 0 through 255 denote Deflate literal bytes, 256 ends the block, and 257 through 285 select lengths. A Deflate backreference is encoded as a length symbol, any length extra bits, a distance symbol, then any distance extra bits. Those extra bits select an offset within the symbol's prescribed range; they are not additional codewords.[ref]
In the illustrative (9,3) Deflate backreference, length 9 uses symbol 263 and distance 3 uses symbol 2; neither needs extra bits. Under the fixed Huffman codes, A, B and C each cost eight bits, symbol 263 costs seven, and distance symbol 2 costs five. Adding the seven-bit end-of-block symbol and three-bit block header gives 3+3⋅8+7+5+7=46 bits, packed into six bytes for a single final block. This is a cost calculation for the explicitly chosen instructions, not a displayed compressed stream.[ref]
Dynamic blocks transmit codeword lengths from which the decoder reconstructs the prescribed prefix codes. The code descriptions themselves use a smaller Huffman code and repeat instructions for successive codeword lengths, including runs of zero lengths. Here run-length encoding describes repeated code lengths, a separate role from copying repeated data bytes. Fixed blocks use predefined Huffman codes and avoid transmitting those descriptions.[ref]

Deflate block framing

Words: 235
Deflate OurBigBook.com
Each block starts with a one-bit BFINAL flag and a two-bit BTYPE field. The BTYPE values are 0 for stored data, 1 for fixed Huffman codes, 2 for dynamic Huffman codes, and 3 for an invalid reserved value. For compressed blocks, symbol 256 ends the current block; BFINAL = 1 says this is the last block. An end-of-block symbol does not mean a literal zero byte, and in a nonfinal block it does not end the whole stream.[ref]
A stored block instead skips to the next byte boundary, reads the sixteen-bit LEN and its sixteen-bit one's complement NLEN, then copies exactly LEN raw bytes. Its length field replaces the compressed block's end-of-block symbol. A compressed block need not end at a byte boundary, so the next block header can start inside the current byte.[ref]
The diagram shows logical fields, not a serialization into bits. RFC 1951 specifies bit packing separately, including different conventions for codewords and other fields (section 3.1.1). For PNG, the filtered image data is compressed inside a zlib wrapper with its own header and checksum; raw Deflate and a complete PNG file therefore have different framing.[ref]

Deflate compression overhead

Words: 227
Deflate OurBigBook.com
Short inputs can spend much of their size on Deflate block framing, the end-of-block symbol and, for dynamic blocks, Deflate Huffman coding descriptions. A repeated phrase is useful only if its Deflate backreference costs less than the Deflate literal bytes it replaces. Huffman coding adapts instruction costs; it does not make either references or code descriptions free.
For an exact expansion example, take the 256 bytes with values 0,1,…,255, each appearing once. A single fixed block containing only Deflate literal bytes costs 144⋅8+112⋅9+7+3=2170 bits, or 272 bytes after final packing. One stored block starting at a byte boundary instead costs five overhead bytes plus the 256 data bytes, or 261 bytes. Both exceed the 256-byte input; these counts follow the specified layouts and are not measurements of an encoder's automatic choice. The example illustrates universal lossless shortening is impossible.[ref]
The following independent experiment obtains an actual raw Deflate stream using the standard library's zlib module, then checks exact recovery. Negative wbits selects raw framing; the three lines of compressed-data handling make no assumptions about which Deflate backreferences the library selects.[ref]
import zlib
data = b"ABCABCABCABC"
encoder = zlib.compressobj(level=6, wbits=-15)
packed = encoder.compress(data) + encoder.flush()
assert zlib.decompress(packed, wbits=-15) == data
print(len(data), len(packed), packed.hex())
The printed bytes describe this library run. Exact roundtrip recovery is the check; a particular compressed length or instruction choice is not a guarantee for other inputs or library versions.

Image compression

Words: 206 Articles: 1
Data compression OurBigBook.com
Image compression applies data compression to pictures, usually represented by raster images. Nearby pixels often have related shades; an encoder can exploit that structure. A flat region invites run-length encoding, while lossy block averaging trades fine detail for fewer stored samples. The choice depends on whether exact pixel values matter and on the patterns in the image.
Lossless source coding recovers the encoded pixel values exactly, including sharp text or numerical image data. Lossy compression preserves an approximation and can remove features that later image processing might need. A visually smooth result is therefore a different promise from exact recovery. Neither method has a universal compression ratio: the chosen file format, its file header and the particular image all matter.
PNG is a real format with lossless source coding of its encoded image data. Its specified compression uses Deflate on reversibly filtered rows, rather than our toy RLE format. The lossy block averaging example is also a teaching format, not a description of PNG. A lossy preprocessing step followed by saving as PNG preserves the already changed pixels, not the earlier original.[ref]

PNG

Words: 47
Image compression OurBigBook.com
PNG is a file format for raster images with lossless source coding of the encoded image data. Its first W3C Recommendation, dated 1 October 1996, described a portable replacement for earlier image formats; this situates the design in exchanging images reliably between systems.[ref]

Software module

Words: 74 Articles: 1
Computer science OurBigBook.com
A software module groups responsibilities behind an application programming interface. Its boundary can be maintained by procedures and hidden storage; it need not be a class in object-oriented programming. Information hiding guides which implementation decisions belong inside that boundary.

Application programming interface

Words: 44
Software module OurBigBook.com
An application programming interface defines the operations available to client code and their promised behavior, including inputs, outputs and failure cases. For a FIFO queue, operation names alone do not specify what happens on an empty or full queue. An API should state those cases before clients depend on them.

Encapsulation (computer programming)

Words: 1k Articles: 7
Computer science OurBigBook.com
Encapsulation bundles related program state and operations or hides implementation details behind an interface. Encapsulation in object-oriented programming realizes this through objects and their permitted operations; encapsulation also applies to modules outside object-oriented programs.
The useful boundary is a promise: clients request operations through an API, and the implementation maintains a representation invariant. Instead of proving that every client updates several storage fields consistently, prove that the permitted operations preserve the representation invariant. Information hiding also leaves room to replace the data structure while keeping the client-facing behavior, a property called representation independence.
Bundling state and operations alone does not establish that promise. Representation exposure can let clients bypass the API. A private annotation alone is not a security guarantee: it does not establish correctness of operations, isolation from hostile code or safe handling of shared mutable storage. The examples below concern sequential calls with no concurrent access and no client access to internal storage; they do not claim protection against arbitrary memory modification.

Information hiding

Words: 170
Encapsulation (computer programming) OurBigBook.com
Information hiding makes an implementation decision the responsibility of one software module, whose API lets other code work without knowing that decision. For a FIFO queue, clients need the removal order and failure behavior; they need not know the current front index in an array. This explains why encapsulation is useful beyond object-oriented programming: procedures with hidden storage can provide the same boundary.[ref]
In On the Criteria To Be Used in Decomposing Systems into Modules by D. L. Parnas (December 1972, pp. 1054–1056), the example applies a sorting algorithm to word rotations of input lines. One decomposition shares storage layouts among processing stages. The alternative exposes line-storage operations such as CHAR and SETCHAR, hiding whether characters are packed four to a machine word. Changing that packing then belongs to line storage rather than every client. The paper presents a design argument using a deliberately small example, not a universal measured speedup or a claim that classes are required. It also notes that an unnecessarily specified rotation order restricts future implementations (p. 1056, Improvement in Circular Shift Module).

Abstract data type

Words: 209 Articles: 2
Encapsulation (computer programming) OurBigBook.com
An abstract data type specifies values and operations independently of their storage. A FIFO queue has ordered sequences as its abstract values; an array and a linked list can represent those same values. A representation invariant identifies valid storage states, and an abstraction function says what each valid state means.[ref]

Representation invariant (I(r))

Words: 105
Abstract data type OurBigBook.com
A representation invariant I(r) specifies which concrete storage states r are valid at the API boundary. Construction must establish it, and each completed operation must preserve it. Internal steps may temporarily violate it only while that state is inaccessible to observers; callbacks or concurrent access would require further reasoning.[ref]
The short proof pattern is mathematical induction on the number of completed calls: the initial state satisfies I; every permitted transition from an I-state ends in an I-state; hence every state observable through the API satisfies I. An unrestricted external write falls outside this argument.

Abstraction function (α:Rvalid​→Q)

Words: 53
Abstract data type OurBigBook.com
An abstraction function maps a valid concrete representation to its abstract value. Write Rvalid​={r:I(r)} and α:Rvalid​→Q. Different storage states can denote the same abstract value. Correct implementation requires both preservation of the representation invariant and agreement with the specified operation after applying the abstraction function; preserving a length bound alone would not prove first-in, first-out behavior.

Bounded queue with encapsulation (0≤∣q∣≤C)

Words: 250
Encapsulation (computer programming) OurBigBook.com
Consider an original FIFO queue example storing immutable labels, with fixed positive integer capacity C. Its abstract state is a finite sequence q=(x0​,…,xn−1​), with 0≤n≤C. The API has enqueue(x), dequeue(), peek() and size(). Successful enqueue returns ok; a full queue returns full and is unchanged. Successful dequeue returns the first label and removes it; an empty queue returns empty and is unchanged. peek returns the first label or empty without modification, and size returns n. The status results are distinct from stored labels.
For a compact array representation (A,n), fix ∣A∣=C and require the representation invariant
I(A,n):n∈Z,0≤n≤C.
(13)
The abstraction function is α(A,n)=(A0​,…,An−1​). Only these first n entries matter; unused slots have no abstract meaning. On successful enqueue(x), write An​=x and then set n←n+1. On successful dequeue(), save A0​, shift the remaining n−1 entries left, and decrement n. Testing the full or empty case before updating gives the specified unchanged failure state.
With C=3 and q=(A,B), enqueue(C) produces (A,B,C); enqueue(D) returns full without change. A raw write n←4 violates the representation invariant. More subtly, changing the count from two to one satisfies its bounds but discards B without a permitted operation. Validity of the storage state and legality of the API transition are different obligations. A setter for every storage field would surrender the useful boundary even if its name looked like an ordinary operation.

Representation exposure

Words: 109
Encapsulation (computer programming) OurBigBook.com
Representation exposure gives outside code access that can modify storage on which the representation invariant or promised behavior depends. Returning the internal array exposes a route around the API; merely hiding the field name does not close it. Incoming shared mutable storage can create the same problem. Copies or immutable values can prevent such modification, but their costs and sharing rules belong in the design.[ref]
The bounded queue with encapsulation deliberately stores immutable labels. A FIFO queue of mutable objects needs a separate promise about whether changing a returned object changes stored content; protecting the queue's ordering and size does not automatically make every stored object immutable.

Representation independence

Words: 339
Encapsulation (computer programming) OurBigBook.com
Representation independence means that clients restricted to the promised API cannot distinguish implementations by the specified results and state transitions. State what observations count: equal returned labels and failure statuses do not imply equal running times, allocations or physical layouts. If the API also promises a resource bound, a replacement must meet that bound too.
Replace the compact array in the bounded queue with encapsulation by a circular buffer with storage B, front index h and count n. Its representation invariant is ∣B∣=C, h,n∈Z, 0≤h<C and 0≤n≤C. Its abstraction function reads the occupied slots using modular arithmetic:
α(B,h,n)=(B(h+i)modC​)i=0n−1​.
(14)
On successful enqueue(x), write B(h+n)modC​=x and increment n. On successful dequeue(), return Bh​, replace h by (h+1)modC and decrement n. Full and empty failures do not alter storage. peek and size have the same abstract meanings as before. Keeping a count distinguishes a full circular buffer from an empty one even when both would have the same next insertion index.
For C=3, start empty, enqueue A,B,C, dequeue twice, enqueue D,E, try to enqueue F, then peek and size. Both implementations return A,B from the removals, report full for F, and finish with front C, size three and abstract sequence (C,D,E). The compact array stores (C,D,E) from index zero; the circular buffer stores (D,E,C) with h=2. Their abstraction functions explain why different stored entries describe the same ordered content.
Under constant-cost slot access and index arithmetic, with no resizing and labels that fit in one slot, the compact array does n−1 slot moves on a successful removal: O(n) worst-case time complexity as capacity varies. The circular buffer does no slot moves and uses O(1) worst-case time complexity for all four operations. Both allocate C slots initially; that construction cost is separate. These are operation-count claims in Big O notation, not measured timings. The short correctness outline checks that each implementation's abstraction function produces the specified new sequence and return value after every successful or rejected call. Repeating that check gives equal traces for clients using only this API.

Hash function (h:U→B)

Words: 2k Articles: 6
Computer science OurBigBook.com
A hash function is a function assigning each key in an input set U a value in an output set B. Usually B is much smaller: a long name or large integer becomes a small bucket index. Equal keys must receive equal values from the same hash function; different keys may also receive equal values. Such a hash collision means "look in the same place", and does not establish key equality. If ∣U∣>∣B∣, the pigeonhole principle makes some collisions unavoidable.
For example, modular arithmetic gives the hash function h(k)=kmod7, with seven bucket indices 0,…,6. Store the seven keys 0,2,3,10,11,17,24: their values are respectively 0,2,3,3,4,3,3. In particular, h(3)=h(10)=3 although 3=10. A hash table is a data structure that uses these indices to locate records. With separate chaining, each bucket holds a linked list of records, so bucket 3 retains all four keys 3,10,17,24. Inserting 10 must not overwrite 3 merely because their hash function values agree.
Searching for 10 computes bucket 3, then compares the actual keys until it reaches 10. Searching for absent key 31 reaches that same bucket and must reject every stored key. This data structure trades a search through all records for a search through one short chain, provided the hash function distributes keys adequately. A fixed hash function can perform poorly on patterned keys: 3,10,17,24 already demonstrate the problem. A universal hash family introduces controlled randomness to limit the expected value of this extra work. Neither indexing nor a small collision probability inherently supplies encryption or message authentication; a cryptographic hash function has additional requirements such as collision resistance.

Hash collision (x=y, h(x)=h(y))

Words: 1k Articles: 1
Hash function OurBigBook.com
A hash collision is a function collision of a hash function h:U→B: two distinct inputs x,y∈U have the same output, h(x)=h(y). Repeating the same input is not a hash collision. Unequal hash values prove the keys differ; equal hash values only identify candidates that might be equal. This makes a hash function useful as a compact filter before comparing the original data.
Here is a deliberately simple example using modular arithmetic. Let h(k)=kmod16 for nonnegative integer keys, and let a four-bucket hash table use the further bucket index b(k)=h(k)mod4. For keys 2,6,18, the hash values are 2,6,2, while all three bucket indices are 2. Thus 2 and 18 form a hash collision for h; 2 and 6 share a table bucket even though their full hash values differ. Always specify which function is being compared: a table collision concerns the bucket-index function, which may discard more information than the original hash function.
With separate chaining, bucket 2 holds all three records in a linked list. A search for 18 visits that bucket and compares the stored keys until it finds 18; a search for 34 visits the same bucket but rejects every stored key. A hash collision changes the search work, while key comparison preserves correctness. Storing only one record per hash value would incorrectly merge distinct keys. This is the purpose of collision handling in a hash table.[ref]
The pigeonhole principle explains inevitability: if a hash function has only M possible outputs, any M+1 distinct inputs contain a hash collision. In particular, a function whose domain of a function is larger than its finite codomain cannot be an injective function. This is an existence statement; it gives neither an efficient way to find the pair nor a probability for a smaller collection of keys. A particular small collection might have no hash collision at all.
For a cryptographic hash function, collision resistance asks that finding any two distinct messages with equal full digests be computationally infeasible under the specified model and resources. It does not mean that hash collisions do not exist. Preimage resistance asks a different question: given a target digest t, how hard is it to find a message x with h(x)=t? The collision finder may choose both messages and their common digest; the preimage finder is given the digest in advance. These definitions distinguish two search tasks, independently of how a hash table stores records.[ref]

Birthday probability for hash outputs (pM​(n)=1−∏j=0n−1​(1−j/M))

Words: 613
Hash collision OurBigBook.com
How soon should a hash collision appear? Specify the probability distribution of the outputs first. Evaluate n distinct keys and assume their hash values Y1​,…,Yn​ are independent random variables, each with the uniform distribution on a finite set of M≥1 possible outputs. The randomness may come from an idealized randomly chosen hash function; a fixed hash function and a fixed list of keys have a definite outcome. Sampling the same key twice creates a repeated hash value without creating a hash collision, so distinctness of the queried keys matters.
This is the existing birthday problem, with hash values in place of birthdays. Let pM​(n) be the probability of at least one equal pair. The exact formula is
pM​(n)=⎩⎨⎧​1−j=0∏n−1​(1−Mj​),1,​0≤n≤M,n>M.​
(15)
The empty product is 1, so pM​(0)=pM​(1)=0. Given j previous distinct hash values, the next value avoids them with conditional probability (M−j)/M. Multiply these conditional chances and subtract from 1. Equivalently, for n≤M, exactly M(M−1)⋯(M−n+1) of the Mn equally likely ordered outcomes have no repeated value. This derivation also explains why independence of all outputs, rather than merely uniform individual values, is required.[ref]
For M=256, the exact hash collision probabilities are p256​(19)≈0.495742, p256​(20)≈0.533167, and p256​(32)≈0.867643. Thus only 20 distinct queries already exceed a one-half chance of some pair matching. The striking feature is the number of opportunities: n queries supply (2n​) pairs. By linearity of expectation, the expected value of the number of equal pairs is λ=(2n​)/M. This expectation counts pairs, not the probability of at least one pair; three equal outputs contribute three pairs in one outcome. The union bound gives pM​(n)≤min(1,λ).
Using the natural logarithm expansion log(1−u)=−u+O(u2) in the exact product gives
pM​(n)≈1−exp(−2Mn(n−1)​).
(16)
For n≤M/2, the omitted correction in the logarithm of the no-collision probability is O(n3/M2). Thus the approximation is controlled when n3/M2 is small; in particular it becomes accurate at the birthday scale n proportional to M​ as M increases. The inequality 1−u≤e−u also shows that the displayed approximation is a lower bound for pM​(n) when n≤M. Setting its exponent to log2 gives the approximate half-probability sample size n≈2Mlog2​ for large M.
For comparison, under the same independent uniform model the probability of hitting one previously fixed digest t in n queries is
qM​(n)=1−(1−M1​)n.
(17)
Each query supplies one chance to hit t, instead of a growing number of possible pairs. For M=256, q256​(20)≈0.075293, and the first integer n with q256​(n)≥1/2 is 178. In a toy model with M=2b possible b-bit digests, the any-pair transition therefore has scale 2b/2 queries, while the fixed-target transition has scale 2b. This explains the birthday-search distinction between collision resistance and preimage resistance.[ref]
The assumptions are essential. Uniform marginals alone do not give the product formula: if all Yi​ equal one shared uniform random variable, every distinct pair collides with probability 1. A universal hash family bounds each pair's hash collision probability, but that condition alone does not supply joint independence of every output. Nor does a fixed output length establish collision resistance or preimage resistance: the toy h(k)=kmod16 has h(k)=h(k+16), making deliberate hash collisions immediate. The curves describe the specified model and do not establish the security of a concrete cryptographic hash function.

Almost strongly universal hash family (Prh​[h(x)=u,h(y)=v]≤ε/q)

Words: 263 Articles: 1
Hash function OurBigBook.com
An almost strongly universal hash family relaxes the exact ordered pair balance of a strongly universal hash family. In the convention used here, choose h with the uniform distribution on a finite set from a family with q possible outputs. Every individual output remains uniform, and for every distinct pair of inputs x,y and every specified ordered pair of outputs u,v,
Prh​[h(x)=u,h(y)=v]≤qε​.
(18)
Equivalently, the conditional probability Prh​[h(y)=v∣h(x)=u] is at most ε. This asks how predictable a second output can become after the first is known.
For q=5, strongly universal hash families give ε=1/5: learning one output leaves each specified second output with conditional probability 1/5. A looser guarantee ε=2/5 permits a specified ordered pair to have probability as large as 2/25, while each individual output still has probability 1/5. Summing over the five equal ordered pairs bounds the collision probability by 2/5, rather than the 1/5 required of a universal hash family. Thus an almost strongly universal hash family need not be a universal hash family. Necessarily ε≥1/q, because the q conditional probabilities sum to one; equality recovers a strongly universal hash family. This relaxation is useful in Wegman–Carter authentication, where efficiency can be traded against a quantified forgery bound within a complete message authentication protocol.

Polynomial almost strongly universal hashing (ha,b​(m)=b+∑j=1L​mj​aj)

Words: 103
Almost strongly universal hash family OurBigBook.com
For fixed-length messages in FqL​, choose independent uniform field elements a,b. Each output is uniform because b masks it. For distinct messages and prescribed output difference d, the equation ∑j=1L​(mj′​−mj​)aj=d is a nonzero polynomial equation of degree at most L, so the root bound for a polynomial gives at most L choices of a. The joint output probability is at most L/q2. Thus the family is (L/q)-almost strongly universal when L<q. Starting the message polynomial at power one matters: using a freely varying message coefficient at power zero would permit a known constant tag shift after observing one tag.

Universal hash family (Prh​[h(x)=h(y)]≤1/q)

Words: 620 Articles: 1
Hash function OurBigBook.com
A universal hash family is a finite collection H of hash functions into an output set of size q such that, for any fixed distinct inputs x,y,
Prh∈H​[h(x)=h(y)]≤q1​.
(19)
The choice of h uses the uniform distribution on a finite set. The keys are fixed before that choice: the randomness belongs to the hash function, so the guarantee does not assume naturally random keys. Choose one member and keep it while using the table; changing it requires redistributing the stored records. The bound holds separately for every distinct pair, without requiring uniform individual outputs or independent random variables. A strongly universal hash family supplies those stronger properties.
The practical payoff follows from linearity of expectation. If n stored keys are distinct from a fixed query, let C count how many share its bucket. Then E[C]≤n/q: each key contributes at most 1/q to the expected value. With 100 stored keys and 100 buckets, an unsuccessful search encounters at most one record on average over the random choice of hash function. This is an expected value, not a limit on every search; one unlucky choice can still create a long chain.
This calculation needs no independence between the collision events: linearity of expectation adds their individual probabilities. The fixed-query condition matters, since deliberately choosing keys after inspecting the selected hash function can target a crowded bucket.
Carter and Wegman introduced this way of analyzing storage and retrieval in their 1977 paper: average over a chosen class of hash functions while allowing any fixed sequence of inputs. Their 1979 journal version develops the same universal-pair collision condition and constructions. The insight is useful because a randomized algorithm can obtain a performance guarantee through its own choices, even when its inputs have inconvenient patterns.[ref][ref]

Strongly universal hash family (Prh​[h(x)=u,h(y)=v]=q−2)

Words: 343
Universal hash family OurBigBook.com
A strongly universal hash family makes every ordered pair of outputs equally likely: for distinct inputs x,y and arbitrary specified outputs u,v,
Prh​[h(x)=u,h(y)=v]=q21​.
(20)
Thus the two outputs are independent random variables, each with the uniform distribution on a finite set. Adding the q equal ordered pairs gives collision probability q/q2=1/q, so the family is also a universal hash family.
Here is a completely enumerable example. In the finite field F5​, take the affine functions ha,b​(x)=ax+b, using modular arithmetic modulo 5. Choose a and b as independent random variables, each with the uniform distribution on a finite set of all five finite field elements 0,1,2,3,4, including a=0. There are 25 equally likely hash functions. For x=0,y=1, the ordered pair is (b,a+b). For instance (a,b)=(2,3) gives (h(0),h(1))=(3,0); (0,3) gives (3,3). Every prescribed (u,v) occurs exactly once, at b=u,a=v−u.
Each row contains five choices, so each individual output has probability 5/25=1/5. Each cell has probability 1/25, and the five diagonal cells give collision probability 5/25=1/5. For any distinct x,y, the same conclusion follows from a=(v−u)/(y−x) and b=u−ax: a nonzero finite field element has a unique inverse. This is the beauty of the construction: two small random coefficients provide exact pair balance without choosing five unrelated values.
The example uses equal-sized input and output sets to make every choice visible; it illustrates the family definitions rather than compression. In a larger input set, a hash function cannot avoid all collisions into five buckets. What a universal hash family controls is the fraction of its members that collide on each fixed pair, rather than the existence of any collision anywhere.
Restricting to a=0 leaves 20 permutations with zero collision probability for distinct inputs. Individual outputs remain uniform, but given h(0)=u, the four values other than u each have conditional probability 1/4 and u has zero. Hence these outputs are not independent random variables: this is a universal hash family but not a strongly universal hash family. Finally, the full 25-member example contains five constant functions, with immediately visible collisions. Its pair guarantee concerns a random choice of hash function, and makes no claim of cryptographic collision resistance.

Conway Game of Life

Words: 1k Articles: 4
Computer science OurBigBook.com
Conway's Game of Life is a cellular automaton in which a simple local rule produces patterns that remain still, pulse, or travel across a square grid. Choose the starting pattern; after that there are no player decisions. The Life blinker and Life glider below make the surprise concrete: the rule mentions only births and survival, yet repeated applications create a clock and a moving shape.
The standard board is infinite, with cells at ordered pairs (x,y)∈Z2 of integers. At generation t∈{0,1,2,…} let at​(x,y) be 1 for a live cell and 0 for a dead cell. Count all eight cells sharing an edge or a corner, excluding the center itself:
nt​(x,y)=∑i,j∈{−1,0,1}(i,j)=(0,0)​​at​(x+i,y+j).
(21)
The local Boolean function defining the next generation is
at+1​(x,y)=⎩⎨⎧​1,1,0,​nt​(x,y)=3,at​(x,y)=1 and nt​(x,y)=2,otherwise.​
(22)
This is the rule B3/S23: a dead cell is born with exactly three live neighbors; a live cell survives with exactly two or three. A live cell with zero or one, or with four through eight, dies. A dead cell with two stays dead. All counts and center states come from generation t: this is a synchronous update, even if an algorithm computes its cells one at a time.[ref]
In particular, the two births in the Life blinker do not help any other cell survive until the following generation. Writing each answer over its old value and then reading that new value for another count changes the rule. The simplest correct algorithm reads one array and writes the next generation into a second array; swap their roles after the entire step. The one-row in-place Life update achieves the same rule with less auxiliary storage by preserving the old values that later counts still need.
A finite implementation must specify its boundary convention. Holding all cells outside the rectangle permanently dead can destroy a Life glider when it reaches the edge. Wrapping neighbor coordinates from one edge to the opposite edge allows interaction with patterns on the other side. Neither convention is the infinite board. The figures display finite windows into an infinite board initially dead everywhere except the stated live cells; the windows do not impose walls.
Conway's Game of Life illustrates emergence in a precise, modest sense: the Life glider's motion is a collective pattern derived from local birth and death, without a motion command. It has deterministic evolution; visually surprising behavior introduces no random choices. Nor do the words "alive" and "dead" make it an experimentally validated model of biology. The beauty is that the same rule yields a stable four-cell square, the Life blinker, and the Life glider: three qualitatively different behaviors from a handful of cells.
For the stable square, take the live set {(0,0),(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)}. Each live cell has three live neighbors, and every dead cell has at most two. The next generation is identical: this configuration is a fixed point of the global update function. In contrast, the Life blinker returns after two generations, and the Life glider returns only after allowing a translation.
The patterns are useful as small, exact checks of an algorithm: the square checks survival without births, the Life blinker checks births and deaths in one simultaneous step, and the Life glider checks several steps and diagonal neighbors. More elaborate constructions can encode data and assemble Boolean circuits; Johnston and Greene develop constructions that simulate arbitrary computation in their chapter 9. This is a statement about suitably designed patterns with enough space and time, not a claim that every starting pattern computes something useful or that a fixed finite board has unlimited computer memory.[ref]
Martin Gardner introduced Conway's Game of Life to his Scientific American readers in October 1970, reporting that Conway selected the rules after experimentation with patterns. The aim was sustained, varied behavior rather than immediate extinction or trivially demonstrable unlimited growth. These were mathematical explorations of chosen rules.[ref]
Gardner's hands-on procedure is still a useful experiment: place black counters for the current live cells; mark doomed counters by stacking another black counter; mark births with white counters; finish checking before removing the doomed stacks and turning white counters black. Count only the original black occupants. Repeat with three adjacent counters to obtain the Life blinker, then with the five coordinates of the Life glider. Recording each generation tests whether the procedure implements the rule; it does not measure a natural population.[ref]

A Life oscillator is a nonconstant periodic orbit of the Conway's Game of Life update function F. Its period is the least positive integer p for which Fp(A)=A, comparing the entire live-cell set at the same coordinates. A configuration that never changes is instead a fixed point; a Life glider is not a Life oscillator on the infinite board because it returns at displaced coordinates. The Life blinker has period two.[ref]

Life blinker (F2(B)=B)

Life oscillator OurBigBook.com
The Life blinker alternates between horizontal and vertical lines of three live cells. Start with B0​={(−1,0),(0,0),(1,0)} and every other cell dead. The two endpoints each have one live neighbor and die; the center has two and survives. The dead cells (0,−1) and (0,1) each have three live neighbors and are born. No other dead cell has three. Therefore
B1​={(0,−1),(0,0),(0,1)},B2​=B0​.
(23)
The same neighbor-count argument with horizontal and vertical exchanged gives the second step. Since B1​=B0​, the period is exactly two, rather than merely a divisor of two.
The Life blinker is a minimal hands-on check of synchronous updating. Mark both endpoints for death and both births before changing anything. Removing an endpoint early would make a prospective birth see only two neighbors; adding a birth early would alter other counts. A correct implementation reproduces both sets above exactly, rather than merely keeping the live population equal to three.

Because the rule uses the same relative neighbors at every position, applying the global update function and applying a translation commute. Thus Gt+4​=Gt​+(1,1) for every generation t; the four-step calculation establishes continued motion on the infinite board. The average displacement is (1/4,1/4) cells per generation, or Euclidean distance 2​/4 per generation. The live-cell count happens to stay five in these frames, but the rule does not conserve live-cell count in general: a single isolated live cell dies immediately. The Life glider persists indefinitely in an otherwise empty infinite board; encounters with other patterns or a finite implementation's edge can change that conclusion.

One-row in-place Life update

Words: 113
Conway Game of Life OurBigBook.com
On a finite rectangular Conway's Game of Life board stored as an array of Boolean variables, retain the preceding row's old values in one auxiliary row. Before overwriting a column, retain rolling sums of the old three-cell vertical columns. Their sum minus the old center is the old neighbor count. Read the next column before changing the current one; replace the saved row entry by the old current cell. The invariant is that every count uses the previous generation, just as in the two-array algorithm. For a board with H rows and W columns this uses O(W) auxiliary storage and O(HW) time. The boundary convention must still be implemented explicitly. The Life blinker and Life glider provide exact expected generations for checking it.

A cellular automaton assigns one of finitely many states to each cell of a regular grid and updates cells in discrete generations using a fixed local rule. In the synchronous convention, each new state depends only on old states in a finite neighborhood. Conway's Game of Life supplies a concrete example with two states and eight neighbors; its global update is a function on complete configurations, with deterministic evolution.[ref]

A computer bus connects components through agreed communication paths and transfer rules. On a shared computer bus, a CPU and a DMA engine can both want the same path to computer memory: attaching another initiator does not create another independent path. Bus arbitration chooses who may start; bus ownership states who may use each resource; bus throughput measures the useful data delivered. This makes sharing a performance question as well as a correctness question.

Shared-bus timing example

Consider a stipulated synchronous shared computer bus, rather than a timing claim about any named hardware protocol. Assume a 32-bit data bus, a 100 MHz clock, and one four-byte payload transfer per bus cycle during the data phase. Both initiators A and B request at time zero. A has one four-transfer write bus burst and B one two-transfer write bus burst, to an immediately ready target in computer memory. Each bus burst pays one bus cycle for bus arbitration and one for its starting address and command; subsequent addresses advance implicitly. The arbiter chooses A first, owners finish their entire bus bursts, and no phases overlap. There are no bus wait states, retries, extra completion cycles, direction changes or intervening requests. Payload is counted when each data phase completes; the observation interval starts at the first bus arbitration cycle and ends at the last payload completion.
A bus cycle lasts
T=100×106 s−11​=10 ns.
(26)
The timeline uses half-open intervals of bus cycles: A has bus arbitration on [0,1), address and command on [1,2), and four payload transfers on [2,6). Then B has bus arbitration on [6,7), address and command on [7,8), and two payload transfers on [8,10). Their final payload completions are at 60 ns and 100 ns respectively. B waits 60 ns before its own selection cycle even though both requests arrived together.
The six payload transfers contain 24 bytes. Ten bus cycles take 100 ns, giving finite-interval bus throughput
R=100 ns24 bytes​=240×106 bytes/s=240 MB/s,

where MB means 106 bytes. The raw data bus rate is 4 bytes×100×106 s−1=400 MB/s. Payload occupies 6/10=60% of the interval. If this same pair repeats with no gaps, its long-run bus throughput equals the finite-interval value; isolated observations need not predict a later workload.
Reverse the bus arbitration order, keeping these assumptions. B finishes after four bus cycles, at 40 ns; A finishes at 100 ns. Aggregate bus throughput stays 240 MB/s, but B's request-to-completion time falls from 100 ns to 40 ns and A's rises from 60 ns to 100 ns. Scheduling changes who waits without changing the available payload capacity in this example.
For an independent perturbation, retain A first and add two bus wait states before B's final payload transfer. The interval grows to 120 ns with the same 24 bytes, so bus throughput falls to 200 MB/s. For another workload, one initiator sends all six transfers in a single bus burst: the stipulated overhead is paid once, giving eight bus cycles, 80 ns and 300 MB/s. This latter comparison assumes one combined request is valid; combining different initiators' operations is not automatically permitted.

Direct memory access

Words: 443 Articles: 3
Computer bus OurBigBook.com
Direct memory access transfers data between a device and computer memory without the CPU executing a copy instruction for each item. The CPU still sets up the operation and observes completion. DMA answers who moves the data; an interrupt answers how a need for attention is announced. A DMA transfer can therefore finish with interrupt-driven input-output or with polled input-output. [ref]
For a toy receive operation, the CPU arranges a four-byte DMA buffer and tells the device its DMA address, length and direction. The device writes the bytes A, B, C, D into that DMA buffer. After completion and any required DMA buffer synchronization, the CPU can read those four bytes. There are four payload bytes, but no four-item CPU copy loop on the device-to-computer memory path. This is a schematic example, not an instruction to operate real hardware.
The useful separation is that the CPU can perform other work while a larger transfer proceeds. The reasoning is a division of responsibilities: setup specifies the destination and extent once; the transfer engine advances through the payload; completion reports the result. The data still crosses an interconnect such as a computer bus, which must share access among competing initiators. Setup, mapping, synchronization and completion cost work, so DMA does not promise a speedup for every transfer size. [ref]
Correctness also requires keeping the DMA buffer alive and coordinating its ownership until the device is finished. A DMA address need not equal a CPU virtual address or physical address. An IOMMU, when present and configured, translates device addresses and can restrict access to authorized computer memory; it is not the CPU's memory management unit. Operating-system process isolation through virtual memory alone does not establish those device-access restrictions. [ref][ref]
