Data structure OurBigBook.com
A priority queue stores items with comparable priority keys and supports insertion, inspection of a best-priority item, and removal of a best-priority item. Here we use the minimum convention: keys have a total order, and smaller means earlier. The operation peek returns a stored item of minimum priority without removing it; extract-min removes and returns such an item. Both require a nonempty priority queue, or an explicitly specified empty-case result. A maximum-oriented priority queue reverses the choice.
For the requests (5,Ada),(2,Bo),(4,Cy), peek returns Bo and leaves all three requests stored. extract-min returns Bo and leaves Ada and Cy; another peek returns Cy. Inserting (1,Dee) now makes Dee the next request selected. This changing collection need not be a sorted array: only the next choice must be available.
Distinct items may share a priority. Inserting (2,Eli) alongside (2,Bo) permits either item to be removed first. A priority queue does not inherently promise arrival order on ties. If that policy matters, compare priority first and a unique increasing arrival number second; the resulting total order makes earlier arrivals win equal-priority ties. This is analogous to the motivation for stable sorting, but it is an extra policy for the priority queue.
The interface specifies behavior; the data structure determines costs. A binary heap implements a priority queue with constant-time peek and logarithmic-time insertion and extract-min, under the cost assumptions below. Scheduling by urgency or by the time of the next event needs exactly this repeated next-item selection. MIT's notes use these applications to motivate the priority queue interface.[ref]

Binary heap

Words: 997 Articles: 3
Priority queue OurBigBook.com
A binary heap represents a priority queue as a complete binary tree obeying a heap order. We use the minimum convention: the priority of every parent in a rooted tree is no greater than the priorities of its children in a rooted tree. Equal priorities are allowed. Each stored entry may be a record carrying a priority key; the numerical example below displays only keys. Reversing the inequalities gives the maximum convention.
The complete binary tree can be stored directly in a zero-indexed array A=(A0​,…,An−1​): read its levels from top to bottom, left to right. The root of a tree is at index 0. The possible children in a rooted tree of index i are at 2i+1 and 2i+2, and an index denotes a present entry only when it is less than n. For i>0, its parent in a rooted tree is at ⌊(i−1)/2⌋, using the floor function. Thus the links of the complete binary tree are determined by arithmetic rather than separately stored pointers.
Consider
A=(2,5,3,9,7,8,4).
(43)
The children in a rooted tree of index 0 have keys 5,3; those of index 1 have keys 9,7; those of index 2 have keys 8,4. The six comparisons 2≤5, 2≤3, 5≤9, 5≤7, 3≤8, 3≤4 establish the heap order. At index 4, the parent in a rooted tree is index ⌊(4−1)/2⌋=1, carrying key 5.
The array is visibly not a sorted array: 5 precedes 3, and 8 precedes 4. Nor is the last entry a maximum: it is 4, whereas the maximum is 9 at index 3. The heap order compares ancestors and descendants, without imposing an order between separate branches. Nevertheless, following the graph path from the root of a tree to any entry gives a chain of nondecreasing priorities. This short argument proves that peek can return A0​, a minimum, without inspecting the other entries.
Insertion appends an entry to the array, preserving the shape of the complete binary tree, then uses sift up to repair the heap order. Insert key 1 into the displayed binary heap. It is appended at index 7, and exchanges with indices 3, 1, then 0:
(2,5,3,9,7,8,4,1)​⟶(2,5,3,1,7,8,4,9)⟶(2,1,3,5,7,8,4,9)⟶(1,2,3,5,7,8,4,9).​
(44)
The moving key follows 7→3→1→0; the keys 9,5,2 each move down one level. Only this chain needs repair.
Now apply extract-min. Save key 1, move the last key 9 to the root of a tree, and shorten the array to length 7. Use sift down, always choosing the smaller of the present children in a rooted tree:
(9,2,3,5,7,8,4)​⟶(2,9,3,5,7,8,4)⟶(2,5,3,9,7,8,4).​
(45)
First 9 exchanges with key 2 at index 1, since 2<3; then with key 5 at index 3, since 5<7. At index 3, the possible children in a rooted tree would be indices 7,8, both outside the shortened array, so the process stops. The returned key is 1, and the remaining binary heap is exactly the original one.
For a nonempty binary heap with n entries, the deepest level is ⌊log2​n⌋, using the floor function and logarithm. Each exchange moves one level and uses only a bounded number of comparisons. The resulting time complexity bounds, expressed in Big O notation, are:
OperationTime complexityReason
peekO(1)Read the root of a tree.
InsertO(logn) for n≥2Append, then sift up through at most the levels of the complete binary tree.
extract-minO(logn) for n≥2Move the last entry, then sift down through at most those levels.
Build from an arbitrary arrayO(n)Apply sift down from the last index with children in a rooted tree back to index 0.
These bounds assume constant-cost indexed access, key comparisons and exchanges, and available array capacity for insertion. Allocating and copying a larger array is a separate cost. Empty and one-entry cases take constant work.
To build a binary heap, begin at index ⌊n/2⌋−1 and work backwards. Entries without children in a rooted tree already obey the heap order. Each sift down, also called heapify down, starts with every present smaller rooted tree below it already repaired. Most entries are close to the bottom and can move very little; successively longer repair distances occur for geometrically fewer entries. Summing these distances gives O(n) work, rather than charging O(logn) to every entry. MIT's notes give this bottom-up construction and contrast it with repeated insertion.[ref]
The Dijkstra algorithm additionally needs to decrease the priority of an existing vertex when its tentative distance improves. Given its current index, lowering the key followed by sift up takes O(logn) time for n≥2. An indexed binary heap maintains a separate map from item identity to its current index and updates that map after every exchange. For vertices numbered in a fixed range, the map can be another array, giving constant-time index lookup. An ordinary unindexed binary heap supplies no such guarantee: locating an arbitrary item can require scanning n entries. Item identity and priority must remain distinct, especially when several vertices have equal tentative distances.
The attractive compromise is local organization with global usefulness. A binary heap maintains only the heap order, yet every extract-min gives the next smallest key. Repeated extraction of the original example gives 2,3,4,5,7,8,9, so a priority queue also supplies a sorting algorithm without storing a sorted array between extractions.

A hash table stores records by key: for example, a product number can select its current stock count without scanning every product. A hash function selects a hash bucket in an array, and a collision-handling method such as separate chaining retains distinct keys assigned to the same hash bucket. The useful idea is to narrow the search to one small collection, while key equality decides which record actually matches.

The absent result must be distinguishable from every permitted stored value. Replacing a value does not increase the record count n. A hash collision between unequal keys must never cause one record to replace the other.[ref]
Let x∼y denote the chosen key equality, an equivalence relation, and let hm​ be the bucket-index hash function for m>0 hash buckets. Correctness requires
x∼y ⟹ hm​(x)=hm​(y),hm​(x)∈{0,…,m−1}.

The converse is false: equal bucket indices merely identify candidates for a key equality comparison. If an implementation first computes a full hash value H(k) and then reduces it to a bucket index, equal keys must have equal H values too. Keep both key equality and the hash function stable while a key is stored; changing the key so it selects another hash bucket can make its record unreachable. α=mn​=44​=1.

Growing this example to m=8 changes the bucket-index hash function: key 5 now belongs to hash bucket 5, while keys 1,9 still share hash bucket 1. Every record must be assigned using the new bucket-index hash function; copying the old array of chain heads unchanged is insufficient. The hash table load factor becomes 4/8=1/2.

Hash table OurBigBook.com
With separate chaining, each hash bucket in a hash table contains a collection of records, often a linked list. Lookup computes the bucket index, then follows that chain until a key equality comparison succeeds or the chain ends. A hash collision therefore affects the search work without merging unequal keys. Deletion searches the same chain and unlinks the matching record; in a singly linked list, remembering the preceding record during the search permits the unlink.[ref]
For the four-key integer example in hash table, insert a new record at the head of its chain after checking that its key is absent. Inserting (1,A),(5,B),(9,C),(2,D) in that order makes hash bucket 1 hold (9,C)→(5,B)→(1,A), hash bucket 2 hold (2,D), and the other two hash buckets empty. All five subsequent operations below select hash bucket 1 because 5mod4=13mod4=9mod4=1:
get(5) rejects key 9, accepts key 5, and returns B after two key equality comparisons. get(13) rejects 9,5,1 and reports absence after three comparisons. put(5,B*) examines 9,5 and replaces the value without changing n=4. delete(9) examines just the head record, removes it, and gives n=3. Finally, put(13,E) rejects 5,1 before inserting the new head record; n returns to 4 and the chain is (13,E)→(5,B∗)→(1,A). The successive hash table load factors are 1,1,1,3/4,1. These counts follow from the stipulated chain order; a different insertion policy changes the successful-search counts.
For a chain of length ℓ, lookup and deletion by key take O(1+ℓ) time complexity in Big O notation. The same applies to put before any resizing, since replacement semantics require checking for an existing equal key. Head insertion alone is O(1) if absence is already known; that is a different precondition. These bounds assume O(1) bucket-index hashing, array access, key equality comparisons, allocation and link updates. A long string or large integer can make hashing or comparison depend on its encoded length, so counting record visits alone does not establish constant running time.
Under simple uniform hashing, each distinct key's bucket index is an independent random variable with a uniform distribution on a finite set of m indices. The keys and query are fixed independently of this random assignment. Then lookup has expected O(1+α) time complexity, where α=n/m is the hash table load factor; it is expected O(1) when α stays bounded. These are model assumptions, not an automatic consequence of using a deterministic hash function.[ref]
Here is the short calculation. For an absent query q and stored keys k1​,…,kn​, let Ii​ be the indicator random variable of hm​(ki​)=hm​(q). The number C of records inspected has expected value
C=∑i=1n​Ii​,E[C]=∑i=1n​E[Ii​]=mn​=α,
(48)
by linearity of expectation. For a present fixed query, scanning its entire chain inspects at most itself plus all other colliding records, with expected value 1+(n−1)/m; stopping at the match only decreases this upper bound. Adding constant hashing and bucket access yields expected O(1+α) for either query. The argument needs pairwise collision bounds; it does not require all the indicator random variables to be independent. A universal hash family can provide a related bound by random choice of a hash function for a fixed key set, as explained in that article.
The worst case remains O(n), and an absent query takes n comparisons if all n records occupy its hash bucket. For instance, 1,1+m,1+2m,…,1+(n−1)m all collide under hm​(k)=kmodm. Separate chaining remains correct, but a sequence of insertions that each checks the existing chain can take quadratic total work. Amortized analysis of resizing does not remove this search cost, and an adaptive choice of keys based on a known hash function is outside the stated simple uniform hashing model.

A fixed-capacity array cannot accept another entry when full. A resizable representation can allocate a larger array and copy the entries. Depth-first search uses this discipline to finish a newly entered branch before resuming the older branch that led to it. Compare the target with the current key: equality returns its value, a smaller target continues into the left subtree, and a larger target continues into the right subtree. Reaching an empty subtree reports absence. The ordering rule justifies discarding the other subtree at every step; this is the algorithm correctness argument for lookup. It applies to the entire subtree, even if that subtree contains many vertices. [ref]

The visited keys are 4→6→5, three key comparisons. The right-child chain stores exactly the same keys and satisfies the same binary search tree rule, but lookup of 5 visits 1→2→3→4→5, five comparisons. Searching for absent key 8 visits 4,6,7 in the first binary search tree and all seven keys in the chain before reaching an empty right subtree.

The binary search tree ordering rule alone does not guarantee this shape or logarithmic time complexity. Breadth-first search also gains no logarithmic key-lookup guarantee merely from having a binary tree: in the displayed balanced example, its left-to-right level order is 4,2,6,1,3,5,7, so it inspects six keys before finding 5, and an absent target requires all seven. Directed lookup uses the total order to choose one branch.
The ordering requirement includes every ancestor on the graph path from the root of a tree. Consider the smaller binary tree with root key 4, left child 2, right child 6, and right child 3 under 2. Key 3 must satisfy both 2<3, from its immediate parent in a rooted tree, and 3<4, from its position in the root's left subtree. Replacing 3 by 5 preserves all immediate parent-child comparisons, including 2<5, but violates 5<4. Lookup for 5 would incorrectly go from 4 to 6 and then to an empty left subtree, overlooking the stored key.
An inorder traversal visits a left subtree, then its own vertex, then a right subtree. On the valid small example its output is 2,3,4,6; on the invalid example it is 2,5,4,6, exposing the descent from 5 to 4. Both seven-key binary search trees yield 1,2,3,4,5,6,7. For a short proof outline, use mathematical induction on the number of vertices: each smaller subtree produces its own sorted list, and the full ordering rule places every left key before the current key and every right key after it. Concatenating these three parts preserves strict order. Sedgewick and Wayne's keys method uses this left-current-right order. [ref]

An abstract syntax tree is a rooted tree recording the meaningful syntactic pieces of a program and how they fit together. A program identifier such as x, a literal value such as 2, and a node representing addition have different roles. Their arrangement answers structural questions: which program expression supplies an operand, which name is a variable assignment target, and which construct encloses another. This makes an abstract syntax tree useful to a compiler, an interpreter, and the type system that checks a program.
The word "abstract" describes what is omitted. Lexical analysis first recognizes lexical tokens, such as x, =, 2, +, 3, *, 4. A concrete parse tree can retain grammar derivation structure, including punctuation and intermediate context-free grammar categories such as expression, term and factor. An abstract syntax tree usually keeps the operation and its operands without all those grammar scaffolds. Parentheses can determine its shape without surviving as separate nodes. A parser may construct the abstract syntax tree directly; it need not first allocate a concrete parse tree.
An abstract syntax tree records programming language syntax, but does not by itself supply all programming language semantics. In a+b, the names do not reveal their current values, and + might perform addition of integers or concatenate strings. The programming language rules, name bindings, and operand types determine the meaning. In Python, successfully calling ast.parse also does not guarantee that later compilation will accept the result: parsing return 42 succeeds, but compiling that statement outside a function fails. [ref]
An abstract syntax tree is not machine code. Its nodes describe language constructs. A compiler can check and transform this structure before translating it into executable instructions; an interpreter can evaluate an appropriate tree directly. The little evaluator below demonstrates this distinction without pretending to implement an entire programming language.

Abstract syntax tree precedence example

Words: 376
Abstract syntax tree OurBigBook.com
Consider Python programs x=2+3*4 and x=(2+3)*4. Operator precedence places multiplication inside the right operand of addition in the first abstract syntax tree. The parentheses instead place addition inside the left operand of multiplication in the second. Their right-hand sides evaluate to 2+(3⋅4)=14 and (2+3)⋅4=20. No rule that simply reads all operators left to right would recover both structures. [ref]
These are schematic views of Python trees: Module is omitted, and the Add/Mult and Store markers are written inside their owning nodes. In the actual schema, BinOp has left, op and right fields; Assign has a list of targets and a value. Name(id='x', ctx=Store()) marks the name as a variable assignment target. Reading x in a program expression instead uses Load. A variable assignment is a statement, not an equation asserting that two values are equal. [ref]
A restricted recursive evaluator can follow those fields. It accepts only integer literal values and binary addition, subtraction and multiplication; the surrounding variable assignment remains a separate action. Using type(value) is int excludes Boolean constants, even though Python treats bool as a subclass of int.
import ast

OPS = {ast.Add: lambda a, b: a + b,
       ast.Sub: lambda a, b: a - b,
       ast.Mult: lambda a, b: a * b}

def evaluate(node):
    if isinstance(node, ast.Constant) and type(node.value) is int:
        return node.value
    if isinstance(node, ast.BinOp) and type(node.op) in OPS:
        return OPS[type(node.op)](evaluate(node.left), evaluate(node.right))
    raise ValueError("outside the integer-expression language")

for source in ("x=2+3*4", "x=(2+3)*4"):
    tree = ast.parse(source, optimize=0)
    statement = tree.body[0]
    print(statement.targets[0].id, evaluate(statement.value))
# x 14
# x 20
The children in a rooted tree have ordered roles: left and right cannot be interchanged. For subtraction, 8-3 gives 5 while 3-8 gives −5. Operator associativity also matters: 8-3-1 parses as (8-3)-1, giving 4, whereas 8-(3-1) gives 6. Here the syntax groups operators to the left; this does not assert the mathematical associativity of subtraction. Operator precedence determines grouping, rather than a general permission to reorder execution. For example, Python evaluates the calls in f()+g()*h() in the order f, g, h, although the multiplication result must be ready before the outer addition. [ref]

An abstract syntax tree traversal systematically visits its nodes. A depth-first traversal of a tree that processes each child before its parent is called postorder. For the program expression 2+3*4, the schematic postorder is 2, 3, 4, Mult, Add. This order lets an evaluator obtain each operand value before applying its operation. A traversal of the entire Python schema additionally visits marker nodes such as Add and Store; this shorter list concerns only the expression nodes drawn in the figures. Visiting an abstract syntax tree is a structural operation, and is not a general model of execution: a conditional may select only one branch, while a structural visitor examines both.

Abstract syntax tree transformation

Words: 310 Articles: 1
Abstract syntax tree OurBigBook.com
An abstract syntax tree transformation replaces or rearranges nodes. It can simplify a program expression, insert instrumentation, or translate a language construct into simpler constructs. When intended to preserve programming language semantics, it must preserve the relevant observable behavior, including values, side effects, and failures. A changed tree can be structurally valid while changing the program's meaning.
Constant folding
Words: 260
Abstract syntax tree transformation OurBigBook.com
Constant folding replaces a program expression whose value is known during translation by a literal value. For x=2+3*4, first replace the multiplication subtree by Constant(value=12), then replace the addition subtree by Constant(value=14). The variable assignment and its Store target survive: the result still assigns to x. This illustrates why a bottom-up abstract syntax tree traversal is convenient: replacing one child can make its parent eligible for the next replacement.
Here is a deliberately small Python transformer. Calling generic_visit first transforms the children; returning a node replaces the visited node. The location helpers retain or supply the metadata expected for compilation. [ref]
class FoldIntegers(ast.NodeTransformer):
    def visit_BinOp(self, node):
        self.generic_visit(node)
        if (isinstance(node.left, ast.Constant)
                and isinstance(node.right, ast.Constant)
                and type(node.left.value) is int
                and type(node.right.value) is int
                and type(node.op) in OPS):
            value = OPS[type(node.op)](node.left.value, node.right.value)
            return ast.copy_location(ast.Constant(value=value), node)
        return node

tree = ast.parse("x=2+3*4", optimize=0)
folded = ast.fix_missing_locations(FoldIntegers().visit(tree))
namespace = {}
exec(compile(folded, "<folded example>", "exec"), namespace)
assert namespace["x"] == 14
assert ast.unparse(folded) == "x = 14"
This transformer folds literal integer operands only. It leaves a+3*4 as a+12, without inventing a value for the program identifier a. It leaves calls intact: replacing 0*f() by 0 could discard a side effect or a failure. Nor does it reassociate floating-point arithmetic, where changing parentheses can change rounding. For the supported integer arithmetic, a short structural induction explains correctness: a retained literal value has the same value; at each folded binary node, the already-correct child values are combined by exactly the original operation in the original left/right order. This claim concerns the supported fragment's values, not unrestricted equivalence of arbitrary Python programs.

Abstract syntax tree source location

Words: 87
Abstract syntax tree OurBigBook.com
An abstract syntax tree can retain source locations even while omitting punctuation nodes. Python records one-based line numbers and zero-based UTF-8 byte offsets, with the end offset exclusive. In x=2+3*4, the multiplication node spans offsets 4 through 7, and ast.get_source_segment returns 3*4. A copied location on a folded 12 describes the original span, not text newly present in the source. Such metadata supports error messages and editing tools without making an abstract syntax tree a lossless record of formatting. [ref]

Type system

Words: 2k Articles: 16
Programming language OurBigBook.com
A type system assigns types to program expressions and supplies rules governing their use. A type constrains permitted operations: in our teaching programming language, int admits integer addition, bool supplies true and false for conditions, and a function type specifies an argument type and a result type. Storage as bits alone does not explain these distinctions; the type system determines whether an expression can serve as an argument, a condition or an operand.
A typing judgment Γ⊢e:τ says that expression e has type τ under the assumptions in the typing context Γ. For example,
Γ={x:int,y:int},Γ⊢x+y:int.
(50)
The assumptions give each operand type int; the addition rule then gives the sum type int. Changing y to type bool prevents this derivation. Our teaching programming language has distinct int and bool types and no implicit conversions between them.
The conditional rule requires a Boolean condition and the same type for both branches:
Γ⊢if c then e1​ else e2​:τΓ⊢c:boolΓ⊢e1​:τΓ⊢e2​:τ​.
(51)
Thus if true then 1 else 2 has type int, while if true then 1 else false is rejected: its branches would require τ=int and τ=bool simultaneously. Even a branch that will not execute is checked by this rule. This is a rule of this particular type system; a different programming language can choose different rules. [ref]
The useful feature is compositional reasoning: after checking the parts, a rule explains how to check the whole. The function type diagram shows this for a call. Type inference can discover the required types automatically, and type variables let one express relationships that recur across many concrete types. The result is both a practical early error detector and a small, readable derivation explaining why an expression fits its intended use.
The guarantee depends on the rules and execution model. Type safety can exclude specified failures such as adding a Boolean or calling an integer as a function. It does not by itself establish every desired runtime property or guarantee that execution terminates. A type system that permits unrestricted recursion can accept a computation that runs forever; exception handling also needs its own account of permitted outcomes.

During type inference, the grammar is extended with type variables such as α for types not yet determined. A type scheme additionally binds such type variables; it is distinct from the individual simple type used at one call.

Type system OurBigBook.com
For a specified programming language and execution model, type safety commonly follows from two properties: a closed expression satisfying a typing judgment is either a value or can take an execution step, and taking a step preserves its type. Proofs proceed by structural induction on derivations, using capture-avoiding substitution for function calls. Repeated preservation keeps the remaining expression typed; the first property then rules out getting stuck at an operation outside the model's permitted cases. This argument does not imply termination or correctness of an arbitrary specification. [ref]

Type variable (α)

Words: 443 Articles: 3
Type system OurBigBook.com
A type variable is a placeholder for a type. In a function type α→α, the repeated type variable requires the argument and result types to agree; α→β does not impose that agreement. A type substitution replacing α by int changes α→α to int→int everywhere within that instance.
For the identity function written as the lambda abstraction λx.x, assume x:α in the body. Looking up x gives result type α, so the abstraction rule gives λx.x:α→α. In the pure Hindley-Milner type system, let identity = λx.x in ... gives identity the type scheme ∀α.α→α by let polymorphism. Each use receives fresh type variables: identity 3 chooses int for its instance, and identity true chooses bool for a separate instance. These choices do not change the original type scheme.
For example, let identity = λx.x in let a = identity 3 in identity true is valid and has type bool. By contrast, (λf. let a = f 3 in f true) (λx.x) is rejected by the Hindley-Milner type system: the lambda abstraction binds f to one monomorphic function type. The first call requires its argument type to be int, and the second requires that same type to be bool. Naming the first result with let a does not generalize f. The distinction makes reusable code possible while keeping the assumptions about a supplied argument consistent.

Words: 43

A type scheme binds type variables that may be instantiated independently at different uses. A free type variable shared with the typing context is not automatically such an independently selectable parameter.
Occurs check
Words: 128
Type variable OurBigBook.com
The occurs check tests whether a type variable occurs inside the expression proposed as its replacement during type unification. After discarding a trivial equation such as α=α, solving α=τ by a type substitution requires that α not occur in τ. Thus α=int→β is permitted when α and β are distinct, but α=α→β is rejected in our finite simple type grammar.
There is a short reason for the rejection. If a finite replacement T for α existed, with replacement B for β, the equation would become T=T→B. The right side's abstract syntax tree has one new arrow node plus the nodes of T and B, so it has strictly more nodes than T. Equal finite type expressions cannot have different sizes. Recursive types are a different design: they explicitly describe self-reference and specify how it interacts with typing judgments.

Cryptography

Computer science OurBigBook.com
The design and analysis of protocols that protect information or authenticate messages in the presence of adversaries. It includes ciphers, digital signatures and cryptographic hash functions.

One-way function

Words: 83 Articles: 1
Cryptography OurBigBook.com
A one-way function is efficiently computable but computationally infeasible to invert on a randomly sampled input with nonnegligible success probability, under its stated security assumption. An RSA cryptosystem supplies the candidate map x↦xemodN on units modulo N. Inversion hardness is an assumption; it is not a proved consequence of merely choosing large primes.

One-way permutation

Words: 31
One-way function OurBigBook.com
A one-way permutation is a bijective one-way function on its input domain. Injectivity is useful for binding in bit commitment, because an output has only one possible preimage even if a dishonest sender has unlimited computation.

Hard-core predicate

Words: 58
Cryptography OurBigBook.com
A hard-core predicate is an efficiently computable bit of an input to a one-way function that cannot be predicted from the function output with nonnegligible advantage over random guessing. For a one-way function f, padding it to F(x,r)=(f(x),r) gives the inner-product predicate h(x,r)=∑j​xj​rj​mod2. This is the Goldreich–Levin construction. It provides a way to mask a bit using an otherwise publicly revealed one-way function value.

Bit commitment

Words: 156 Articles: 1
Cryptography OurBigBook.com
A bit commitment allows a sender to fix a bit while concealing it from the receiver until an opening phase. Binding prevents a sender from opening the same commitment as either bit; hiding prevents the receiver from learning the bit prematurely. With a one-way permutation F and a hard-core predicate h, a commitment can consist of F(x) and the masked bit b⊕h(x). Opening reveals x. Injectivity gives binding, while unpredictability of the hard-core predicate gives computational hiding. For an RSA cryptosystem, the receiver must not possess the inverse trapdoor.

Ensemble-steering attack on quantum bit commitment

Words: 71
Bit commitment OurBigBook.com
If the two honest quantum state ensembles have the same density operator, their independently prepared blocks are perfectly hiding. A dishonest sender can instead send one half of a purification of a density operator and retain the other. The Hughston–Jozsa–Wootters theorem allows a measurement of the retained system to prepare either honest ensemble after commitment. If verification checks only the declared states, either opening is then accepted with the honest probabilities. This gives a concrete failure of binding while preserving perfect hiding.

Quantum key distribution

Words: 190 Articles: 1
Cryptography OurBigBook.com
Quantum key distribution uses a quantum channel and an authenticated public classical channel to establish matching random keys for two parties while limiting an eavesdropper's information. The public transcript is included in the adversary's information. In an ideal successful protocol, a key of length ℓ is uniform and independent of that information. Actual protocols allow small disagreement and secrecy errors and may abort. Measurement in quantum mechanics disturbance provides parameter tests, while privacy amplification removes residual knowledge after classical reconciliation. The BB84 protocol and entanglement-based protocols are examples.

Premature basis announcement in quantum key distribution

Words: 110
Quantum key distribution OurBigBook.com
If basis information and test positions are announced before the receiver confirms receipt of quantum carriers, an eavesdropper can store the carriers until learning that information. In a scheme sending one half of each Bell pair after a Hadamard gate encoding, the eavesdropper then forwards test qubits untouched and measures all data qubits in their now-known correct bases. Every test passes, while data are changed to classically correlated product states whose bit labels the eavesdropper knows. This invalidates the sampling argument needed to justify entanglement purification and quantum key distribution. A sound additional purification certification could detect this attack and abort; it cannot generate private Bell pairs from the separable attacked data. Announcing bases only after receipt prevents this particular delayed-carrier attack.

Cryptography OurBigBook.com
A protocol for two distant parties to agree on a random bit without trusting either party to announce an unverified coin toss. In the Rabin-Williams scheme, a publicly committed square hides which of two half-interval roots the sender selected. The other party guesses a digit distinguishing those roots; subsequent root and factor revelations verify the completed exchange. The protocol's fairness relies on prescribed randomness and the difficulty of finding a second root; it does not force a party to complete communication.

Privacy amplification compresses a partially secret random string into a shorter key by a publicly selected hash function, reducing an adversary's information about the final key. In the BB84 protocol it follows parameter estimation and error correction, and accounts for information leaked in the public reconciliation transcript. Authentication of the public channel remains necessary.

Algorithm

Words: 7k Articles: 52
Computer science OurBigBook.com
An algorithm is a finite, precise procedure for transforming an input into an output.
Here "finite" refers to the description: a short algorithm can perform arbitrarily many steps on increasingly large inputs. Solving a computational problem additionally requires termination and the specified output on every permitted input. State assumptions explicitly: binary search requires a sorted array.
An algorithm is an idea that can have implementations in different programming languages. Its explanation should make three things visible: the permitted inputs, the rule for each step, and the meaning of the returned output. Algorithm correctness then separates finding the right answer from eventually finishing; time complexity asks how much work finishing requires.
A particularly useful design question is: what knowledge survives each step? In binary search, it is the location of every possible match inside the remaining candidate range. Writing that fact as a loop invariant turns an intuitive shortcut into a procedure whose discarded candidates can be justified. This often helps discover the algorithm, rather than merely check it afterward.

Depth-first search

Words: 581
Algorithm OurBigBook.com
Depth-first search is a graph search that follows a branch as far as it can before returning to try the next unexplored branch. Starting at a vertex s of an undirected graph on a finite set of vertices, mark s as discovered. Scan its graph neighbours in a fixed order: for each undiscovered vertex, record the current vertex as its parent in a rooted tree in the discovery tree, mark the new vertex, and explore it immediately using recursion. Return when its adjacency list is exhausted. Discovery marks persist after return, preventing a graph cycle from causing repeated exploration. This branch-and-return rule is the maze exploration described in MIT's notes. [ref]
Use the same unweighted undirected graph as breadth-first search, with vertex set V={A,B,C,D,E,F,G} and edges
E={AB,AC,BD,BE,CE,CF,EG,FG},
(55)
where XY denotes the unordered pair {X,Y}. Visit graph neighbours in lexicographic order of their one-letter labels, starting at A. The discovery order, computed by the diagram's generator, is
A,B,D,E,C,F,G.
(56)
The discovery edges in order are AB,BD,BE,EC,CF,FG. They form a rooted tree spanning the reached vertices, with root of a tree A. The other edges, AC and EG, remain in the original graph but never discover a new vertex. In particular, the graph cycle A,B,E,C,A causes no repeated discovery.
At D there is no undiscovered graph neighbour, so its call returns to B. The next call enters E, then C, then F, then G. Immediately after discovering G, the call stack is A,B,E,C,F,G, with G on top; D is still discovered but its call has finished. The maximum call stack depth is six, although seven vertices are discovered. Following the recorded parent in a rooted tree backwards at each step reconstructs a graph path; here the route from A to G is A,B,E,C,F,G, using five edges. Breadth-first search instead finds A,B,E,G, using three edges. Depth-first search establishes reachability but does not guarantee the fewest edges.
An explicit LIFO stack can replace recursion, but its entries and discovery rule must be specified. To reproduce this exact traversal, store one frame per active vertex, retaining the next position in its adjacency list. Advance the top frame by one graph neighbour; if that vertex is undiscovered, mark it and push its frame immediately; pop an exhausted frame. Pushing all undiscovered graph neighbours at once and marking them on push is a different iterative variant. Even pushing them in reverse lexicographic order does not generally reproduce the parent in a rooted tree relationships above: C would already be marked while processing A, so E could not discover C.
With an adjacency list representation, constant-cost discovery checks and frame operations, and the graph neighbours already ordered, depth-first search has time complexity O(∣V∣+∣E∣) in Big O notation. Each reached vertex is entered once and each incident edge is examined at most twice in an undirected graph; initializing all discovery marks costs O(∣V∣). The call stack has depth at most ∣V∣, since no active vertex repeats. Discovery marks and the recorded parent in a rooted tree for each nonroot vertex also need O(∣V∣) auxiliary space complexity, excluding storage for the graph. Sorting adjacency lists to obtain a chosen order is additional work. [ref]
One start explores only its connected component of a graph. To cover a disconnected graph, start again at every still-undiscovered vertex while keeping all discovery marks; the discovery trees form a forest. Depth-first search is useful for reachability, constructing a spanning tree of a connected graph, and organizing the return steps needed by a depth-first traversal of a tree. For detecting a graph cycle in a simple graph that is an undirected graph, an edge to an already discovered vertex other than the current parent in a rooted tree closes a graph cycle; the immediate return edge to that parent in a rooted tree is not itself a graph cycle.

Memoization

Words: 1k Articles: 6
Algorithm OurBigBook.com
Memoization retains a completed function result under a memoization key and returns that result when an equivalent request recurs. For a terminating pure function, repeated evaluation can therefore become lookup rather than repeated work. The benefit is especially striking with recursion and overlapping subproblems: a large tree of calls can refer to a small Directed acyclic graph of distinct answers. The memoization cache contract determines whether reuse is correct; the memoization cache lifetime determines whether an answer is still present when wanted.
Memoization records computed answers, whereas a memory cache retains data from computer memory. A CPU cache hit does not by itself prevent a program from evaluating the same function again. Spreadsheet dependency evaluation adds an explicit mechanism for invalidating affected cached cell values after inputs change; a general memoization table does not discover such changes automatically.
A documented early motivation was to let programs improve their efficiency during execution through rote learning: the abstract of a 1968 paper explicitly proposes such a programming language facility.[ref]

Overlapping subproblems

Words: 58
Memoization OurBigBook.com
Overlapping subproblems occur when several parts of a calculation request the same smaller problem. Memoization can share its answer if the memoization key identifies that problem completely. For the Fibonacci numbers, both F5​ and F4​ require F3​. In dynamic programming, the dynamic programming state plays the corresponding role of identifying a reusable continuation. Overlap explains potential savings; the recurrence relation and its base cases still need to be correct.

Memoized Fibonacci evaluation (Fn​)

Words: 460
Memoization OurBigBook.com
The Fibonacci numbers give an exact example. For a nonnegative integer n, their recurrence relation is
F0​=0,F1​=1,Fn​=Fn−1​+Fn−2​(n≥2).
(57)
To obtain F5​=5 by direct recursion, evaluate F4​ and F3​ separately; computing F4​ also evaluates F3​. The full call tree has 15 occurrences but just six distinct arguments, 0,1,2,3,4,5. Shared dependencies form a Directed acyclic graph because every directed edge goes to a strictly smaller argument. Memoization evaluates a distinct argument on first demand; filling values in increasing argument order is the corresponding bottom-up dynamic programming calculation.[ref]
Use an initially empty hash table memo, shared by every recursive call. Count even the first evaluations of the two base cases, store only completed results, evaluate the left term first, and retain all entries. The following original procedure assumes a nonnegative integer argument:
def cached_fib(n, memo):
    if n in memo:
        return memo[n]
    if n < 2:
        value = n
    else:
        value = cached_fib(n - 1, memo) + cached_fib(n - 2, memo)
    memo[n] = value
    return value
Every self-call must pass through the memoization lookup. Wrapping only the outer call while leaving inner calls uncached retains the repeated work. Test membership rather than whether the stored value is nonzero: F0​=0 is a valid completed result.
For cold F5​, the lookup arguments are 5,4,3,2,1,0,1,2,3. The first six are absent; the last three reuse completed answers. Results are stored on return in argument order 1,0,2,3,4,5, with values 1,0,1,2,3,5. Thus there are nine wrapper calls, six body evaluations and four additions. Repeating F5​ with the same table takes one wrapper call and no body evaluation. Requesting F6​ next evaluates only its body, reuses F5​ and F4​, and stores F6​=8: three wrapper calls, one body evaluation and two hits.
The direct-call count satisfies C0​=C1​=1 and Cn​=1+Cn−1​+Cn−2​. Its exact solution is Cn​=2Fn+1​−1, as substitution into this recurrence relation verifies. With the specified memoization procedure, a cold call at n≥2 evaluates n+1 distinct bodies, makes n−1 additions and makes 2n−1 wrapper calls. There are n−2 hits: each of the n−1 nonbase bodies issues two recursive calls, in addition to the initial call. The difference is between the number of occurrences and the number of distinct subproblems.

Memoization arithmetic and stack costs

Words: 208
Memoization OurBigBook.com
Under constant-cost lookup and integer addition, Memoized Fibonacci evaluation has time complexity O(n) in Big O notation, retaining O(n) values. A hash table needs its own lookup-cost assumptions; an array indexed by 0,…,n avoids hash collisions in this example. Memoization removes repeated bodies, but also pays for keys, lookups and retained answers. A workload without reuse can pay those costs without saving evaluations.
The call stack remains. Left-first recursion descends through arguments n,n−1,…,1 before returning, giving n simultaneously active frames for n≥2. Therefore the auxiliary space complexity includes O(n) frames as well as O(n) table entries in the constant-size-value model. An iterative bottom-up dynamic programming calculation removes these recursive frames; retaining only the two previous Fibonacci numbers suffices when only the final value is wanted, but discards the table useful for later requests.
Exact Fibonacci numbers do not remain constant-size values. For k≥2, the recurrence relation gives 2(k−2)/2≤Fk​≤2k−1, so the representation of Fk​ as a binary number has order k bits. With ordinary addition costing order k bit operations on such operands, the n−1 additions cost order n2 bit operations in total. Retaining all values also requires order n2 bits of value storage, before keys and frame overhead. The linear bound counts additions under its stated cost model; it is not a linear bound on exact integer arithmetic in bits.[ref]

Memoization cache contract

Memoization OurBigBook.com
For a terminating pure function, a reusable entry must record its correct completed result, and equal memoization keys must imply equal results throughout the entry's memoization cache lifetime. Reusing that result must also preserve the behavior callers require. These conditions separate correctness from speed: a complete key can be correct even if it rarely repeats.
A procedure using deterministic computation can still have a required side effect. If a procedure returns n2 and appends an audit record on every call, serving the second call from a table preserves the numerical answer but skips the second record. Likewise, if each call promises a fresh mutable list, returning the same stored mutable list changes observable sharing and allows a caller to damage later answers. Plain result reuse is unsuitable for those contracts.[ref]
Completion matters for recursion. Suppose computing key A needs key B, and computing B needs A. A table containing only completed answers has no answer to return for the second A; remembering completed values does not make this directed cycle terminate. Marking a key ACTIVE before descending detects re-entry, as in spreadsheet dependency evaluation, but detection is not a solution of the circular equations. If computation fails, clear its active mark and do not publish an unfinished value. The example using Fibonacci numbers avoids this issue through a strictly decreasing argument.
The call counts above assume sequential execution and no eviction. Concurrent requests for an absent key can both begin evaluation before either publishes its result; keeping a table coherent alone does not ensure one body execution per key.[ref]
Memoization key (K(x,c))

A memoization key identifies all information that determines a reusable answer. Write x for explicit arguments and c for relevant context. For a function f and key function K, the necessary value condition is
K(x,c)=K(y,d) ⟹ f(x,c)=f(y,d).
(58)
This implication need hold only for contexts in which the entry can be reused. The condition concerns key equality, not merely equality of hash function outputs: a hash table must resolve hash collisions by comparing complete keys. Include the identity or version of the procedure if one table stores results for several procedures or changing implementations.
For an original toy example, let g(n,a)=an. Caching only by n after g(3,2)=6 incorrectly returns 6 for g(3,4), whose answer is 12. The pair (n,a) is complete for this function. If a is hidden in mutable configuration, either freeze that configuration for the memoization cache lifetime, include a reliable version in the key, or invalidate affected entries before reuse. A version is sufficient only if every relevant change updates it. Object identity alone is likewise insufficient for a mutable list whose contents determine the answer.

Memoization cache contract OurBigBook.com
A memoization cache lifetime is the interval over which retained entries are available and valid. One table per top-level request shares recursive subproblems within that request; keeping a table between requests also allows the warm F5​ and incremental F6​ examples. Clearing it loses those savings. Evicting a correct answer can preserve correctness for a terminating pure function, while forcing recomputation; changing an input without invalidating an obsolete answer can break correctness.
Specify who owns the table, when context changes invalidate it, and how long keys and results occupy computer memory. In a concrete implementation, retained references can keep arguments and answers alive until removal or clearing.[ref] The memoization promise is conditional reuse of valid completed answers, not an automatic guarantee of freshness, termination or bounded computer memory.

Recursion (computer science)

Words: 48
Algorithm OurBigBook.com
Recursion solves a problem by invoking the same procedure on smaller instances, with base cases answered directly. For merge sort, an empty or one-entry array is already sorted, and every larger array is split into two shorter parts. The decreasing lengths justify termination; a self-call without a progress rule would not suffice.

Divide-and-conquer algorithm

Words: 45
Algorithm OurBigBook.com
A divide-and-conquer algorithm divides a problem into smaller instances, solves them using recursion, and combines their answers. In merge sort, the division makes two contiguous halves, and the merge algorithm combines the resulting sorted arrays. The important design step is finding a combination rule cheaper than solving the whole problem afresh.

Sorting algorithm (B0​≤B1​≤⋯≤Bn−1​)

Words: 2k Articles: 11
Algorithm OurBigBook.com
A sorting algorithm rearranges a finite sequence into nondecreasing order under a chosen total order on its keys. Its output must contain every input entry exactly once, including repetitions: producing ordered values is insufficient if entries are lost. Merge sort is one such algorithm; stable sorting adds a requirement about equal keys.
Sorting creates reusable structure: equal sort keys become adjacent, and a sorted array supports binary search. However, an algorithm correctness check must establish both sortedness and sorting permutation preservation. Replacing every entry by the smallest key can produce ordered keys while destroying the original data. Stable sorting imposes a third condition when equal sort keys occur: retain their arrival order.
For example, take complete sorting records (2,A),(1,B),(2,C),(1,D), with the first component as the sort key and the letter as associated data. A correct output is (1,B),(1,D),(2,A),(2,C). The sort keys are ordered, every complete sorting record remains, and the equal-key pairs keep A before C and B before D. The output (1,D),(1,B),(2,C),(2,A) satisfies sortedness and sorting permutation preservation, but fails stable sorting. The output (1,B),(1,B),(2,A),(2,A) has the right multiset of sort keys but loses C,D and duplicates A,B; it fails sorting permutation preservation of complete sorting records.
To express stable sorting precisely, label every input occurrence by its original position, even when two complete sorting records have identical contents. Let p(i) be the output position of the occurrence originally at position i. Besides sortedness and sorting permutation preservation, require
i<j and k(Ai​)=k(Aj​)⟹p(i)<p(j).
(59)
Here k is the sort key function. Sorting by the pair (k(Ai​),i) under lexicographic order gives the same order as stable sorting by k: the original position breaks ties without discarding associated data. For a two-field ordering, first apply stable sorting by the secondary sort key, then apply stable sorting by the primary sort key. The second pass retains the secondary order within each group of equal primary sort keys. For instance, (2,B),(1,C),(2,A),(1,A) first becomes (2,A),(1,A),(2,B),(1,C) by letter, then (1,A),(1,C),(2,A),(2,B) by number.

Sorting algorithm OurBigBook.com
A sort key is the value extracted from a complete entry to determine its ordering. Model extraction as a function k into a total order; compare k(Ai​) and k(Aj​), while moving the complete entries. Ordering sorting records by an age field does not also compare their names. Repeated sort keys are allowed, so this induces equal-key groups even when the complete sorting records differ. Keep the sort key function and the comparison rule fixed throughout a sort; inconsistent comparisons need not admit any sorted result.

A complete entry comprising a sort key together with any associated data. In (2,A), the sort key is 2 and A stands for the associated data or an identity label. Sorting permutation preservation concerns these complete entries, rather than only their extracted sort keys.

Sortedness (k(Bi​)≤k(Bi+1​))

Sorting algorithm OurBigBook.com
For an output sequence B of length n, sortedness means
k(Bi​)≤k(Bi+1​)(0≤i<n−1)
(60)
under the chosen total order on sort keys. Its transitivity also gives k(Bi​)≤k(Bj​) whenever i<j. An empty sequence and a one-entry sequence satisfy sortedness without any adjacent comparison. For longer sequences, checking adjacent pairs suffices; checking only the first and last sort keys does not. For example, (1,3,2,4) passes an endpoint comparison but fails sortedness at 3,2. Sortedness alone says nothing about which input entries survived.

Sorting permutation preservation (Bi​=Aπ(i)​)

Words: 88
Sorting algorithm OurBigBook.com
The output of a sorting algorithm must be a permutation of the complete input sequence. For equal lengths n, require a permutation π of {0,…,n−1} such that
Bi​=Aπ(i)​(0≤i<n).
(61)
Equivalently, the input and output have the same multiset of complete entries: each entry has the same multiplicity. Equality of the underlying sets is insufficient; (1,1,2) and (1,2,2) have the same set of values and the same length but different multisets. When tracking occurrences rather than contents, retain original identity labels to check that each one is moved exactly once. A swap preserves this multiset automatically; an overwrite need not.

Insertion sort

Words: 321
Sorting algorithm OurBigBook.com
Insertion sort grows a sorted prefix of an array one entry at a time. In the adjacent-swap version, start with position i=1, compare its current sort key with the preceding sort key, and swap the complete sorting records only when the right sort key is strictly smaller. Continue leftward until no swap is needed or the entry reaches position zero; then process original position i+1. A tie stops the pass. This is the strict comparison and exchange rule in the authored implementation.[ref]
Take A=(2A​,1B​,2C​,1D​), where the subscript labels a complete sorting record and comparisons inspect only its sort key. Starting from index zero, the complete key-comparison trace is:
ComparisonRight sort key smaller than left?ActionArray after the action
1, insert position 11B​<2A​: yesSwap positions 0,1.(1B​,2A​,2C​,1D​)
2, insert position 22C​<2A​: noStop this pass on a tie.(1B​,2A​,2C​,1D​)
3, insert position 31D​<2C​: yesSwap positions 2,3.(1B​,2A​,1D​,2C​)
4, continue leftward1D​<2A​: yesSwap positions 1,2.(1B​,1D​,2A​,2C​)
5, continue leftward1D​<1B​: noStop this pass on a tie.(1B​,1D​,2A​,2C​)
The loop invariant is that, before pass i, positions 0,…,i−1 satisfy sortedness and contain precisely the entries originally in that prefix. Moving the next entry left through strictly larger sort keys extends that prefix, and every swap retains sorting permutation preservation. Equal-key entries never cross, giving stable sorting. Each leftward step decreases the position, and each completed pass increases the prefix length, so the algorithm terminates.
With constant-cost key comparisons and swaps, reverse-ordered distinct sort keys cause 1+2+⋯+(n−1)=n(n−1)/2 comparisons and swaps. Thus worst-case time complexity is O(n2) in Big O notation. An already sorted array needs only n−1 key comparisons for n≥1 and no swaps. The adjacent-swap version uses constant auxiliary space complexity. Small or nearly sorted arrays can therefore make insertion sort useful despite its quadratic worst case.

Comparison sort

Words: 332 Articles: 1
Sorting algorithm OurBigBook.com
A comparison sort learns the ordering of sort keys only by comparing pairs. The keys are otherwise opaque: their numeric values, digits or encodings cannot choose an array index or a branch. It may move complete sorting records and retain previous answers. Merge sort and the adjacent-swap insertion sort are comparison sorts; counting sort and radix sort exploit additional information.
Comparison sorting lower bound (Cmax​(n)≥⌈log2​(n!)⌉)
Words: 288
Comparison sort OurBigBook.com
Any deterministic comparison sort correct for all orders of n distinct sort keys needs at least ⌈log2​(n!)⌉ comparisons on some input. Here n! is a factorial, log2​ a logarithm, and the brackets denote the ceiling function. This is a worst-case requirement, not a requirement on every input.[ref]
For three distinct sort keys, the diagram has one leaf for each possible ordering of the original entries a,b,c. Some paths need two comparisons, others three; two comparisons cannot distinguish all six orders.
For the proof outline, represent adaptive comparisons by a binary tree: distinct sort keys give only two outcomes per comparison. A leaf fixes an output permutation; one leaf cannot correctly handle two different strict orders. Hence there must be at least n! leaves. Maximum depth h permits at most 2h leaves, so 2h≥n! gives the bound. Even a three-way comparator has only two reachable outcomes on this distinct-key family.
The growth follows without a precise approximation to the factorial. At least ⌊n/2⌋ of its factors are at least n/2, so for n≥2,
log2​(n!)≥⌊n/2⌋log2​(n/2).
(62)
The brackets denote the floor function. This gives a constant times nlogn lower bound for large n, matching the worst-case comparison growth of merge sort.
Distinct sort keys are essential to the n! counting argument. Identical sort keys do not create n! different strict orders. If all sort keys coincide, stable sorting returns the arrival order. This does not remove the worst-case bound for a comparison sort required to handle arbitrary distinct-key inputs.

Counting sort (T(n,K)=O(n+K))

Words: 61
Sorting algorithm OurBigBook.com
Counting sort uses integer sort keys in {0,…,K−1} directly as indices into an array of counts. Constant-cost counting and indexing give O(n+K) time complexity in Big O notation. To retain complete sorting records, cumulative counts locate their output ranges; filling each range from its end while scanning the input backwards gives stable sorting. Emitting bare sort keys from counts would discard associated data. The K term matters when the key range is large.[ref]

Radix sort (T(n,d,R)=O(d(n+R)))

Words: 71
Sorting algorithm OurBigBook.com
Radix sort sorts encoded sort keys a digit at a time. Its least-significant-digit version uses stable sorting on each successive digit, often by counting sort. For d digits with R possible values each, it takes O(d(n+R)) time complexity in Big O notation, assuming constant-cost digit extraction and indexing. Stable sorting retains the ordering established by earlier digits when a later digit ties. Both digit access and the direct indexing in counting sort lie outside the comparison sort model, so these bounds do not contradict the comparison sorting lower bound.[ref]

Stable sorting

Words: 59
Sorting algorithm OurBigBook.com
Stable sorting preserves the original relative order of entries with equal keys. The entries may carry different names or other information even when their keys coincide. For example, sorting records (2,Ada),(1,Bo),(2,Cy) by the numerical key gives (1,Bo),(2,Ada),(2,Cy): Ada remains before Cy. This is useful when a previous ordering contains information worth retaining, such as arrival order among equally ranked requests.

Merge sort (T(n)=O(nlogn))

Words: 612
Sorting algorithm OurBigBook.com
Merge sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm that sorts a finite array by splitting it into contiguous halves, sorting each half using recursion, and combining the two sorted arrays with the merge algorithm. An empty or one-entry array is returned immediately. For length n≥2, put the first ⌊n/2⌋ entries on the left and the remaining ⌈n/2⌉ on the right; the brackets are the floor function and ceiling function. Always choose the left head on equal keys to obtain stable sorting. This is the split, sort, combine structure taught in the MIT lecture notes.[ref]
Take the concrete input array
A=(7,2a​,5,2b​,9,1,4,3).
(63)
The tags identify the entries originally at indices 1 and 3, counting from zero. Both keys are 2; the tags are never compared. Reading downward in the figure follows the splits, then the returned sorted arrays. Arrows show dependencies; the level layout groups independent calls rather than giving their chronological execution order.
The first two halves are (7,2a​,5,2b​) and (9,1,4,3). Their pairs split into one-entry base cases. Applying the merge algorithm gives the following fully worked return levels; each number in the last column counts only comparisons between two available heads.
Returning levelResulting sorted arraysHead comparisons
Pairs(2a​,7), (2b​,5), (1,9), (3,4)1+1+1+1=4
Halves(2a​,2b​,5,7), (1,3,4,9)3+3=6
Whole array(1,2a​,2b​,3,4,5,7,9)7
In the left-half merge algorithm, the head pairs are (2a​,2b​), (7,2b​) and (7,5); it takes 2a​,2b​,5, then appends 7. In the final merge algorithm, the head pairs are (2a​,1), (2a​,3), (2b​,3), (5,3), (5,4), (5,9) and (7,9). It takes 1,2a​,2b​,3,4,5,7, then appends 9. Thus this precise version makes 4+6+7=17 head comparisons and, ignoring identity tags, returns (1,2,2,3,4,5,7,9).
The elegance of merge sort is that it creates exactly the structure its next step needs: two smaller sorted arrays make the larger ordering inexpensive. Once the whole array is sorted, equal keys are adjacent and binary search can serve repeated queries. Stable sorting also retains information that the keys alone do not express. If the left-half merge algorithm instead takes the right head on the 2a​=2b​ tie, it returns (2b​,2a​,5,7); the keys are sorted but stable sorting has failed.
For time complexity, assume each key comparison, entry access and entry copy has constant cost. The merge algorithm processes n entries in O(n) time. In Big O notation, the resulting recurrence relation is
T(0),T(1)=O(1),T(n)=T(⌊n/2⌋)+T(⌈n/2⌉)+O(n)(n≥2).
(64)

For arbitrary n, there are at most ⌈log2​n⌉ returning levels, each processing at most n entries, giving the same bound. The worst-case number of head comparisons is also O(nlogn). Here log2​ is the base-two logarithm. The MIT notes give this level-by-level analysis for merge sort.[ref]
The conventional array implementation uses a reusable buffer of n entries for the merge algorithm, together with O(logn) pending calls for recursion. Its auxiliary space complexity is therefore O(n), beyond the original array. This bound describes that implementation. A linked list permits a merge algorithm that reconnects existing nodes; its storage accounting differs from copying array entries into a buffer.
For a short algorithm correctness outline, the empty and one-entry base cases are sorted. Assuming recursion correctly sorts both shorter halves, the merge algorithm returns all their entries in order. Equal keys within a half keep their relative order by the same argument applied to the smaller call; across halves, every left entry originally preceded every right entry, so taking left first preserves stable sorting. Both half-lengths decrease for n≥2, establishing termination.

Merge algorithm (C(m,n)≤m+n−1(m,n≥1))

Words: 410
Algorithm OurBigBook.com
The merge algorithm combines two finite sorted sequences under the same total order, retaining every entry exactly once. Keep a position at the first unconsumed entry, or "head", of each input. While both heads exist, compare their keys, append the smaller head to the output, and advance only that head's position. On equality take the left head. Once either sequence is exhausted, append the other remainder without further key comparisons. Empty inputs therefore require no head comparisons. The MIT notes illustrate this two-head combination step.[ref]
For example, the merge algorithm applied to (1,4,7) and (2,3,8,9) returns (1,2,3,4,7,8,9):
The head pairs (1,2), (4,2), (4,3), (4,8) and (7,8) select 1,2,3,4,7 respectively. After the fifth comparison the left sequence is empty, so (8,9) is appended. Seven entries are written, but only five head comparisons occur: tests for exhaustion and appending the remainder are separate operations. This distinction makes the example's count smaller than the bound 3+4−1=6.
For nonempty inputs of lengths m,n, each head comparison consumes exactly one entry. After m+n−1 such removals at most one entry remains, so both heads cannot still exist. Hence the merge algorithm uses at most m+n−1 head comparisons. The bound can be attained: (1,3,5) and (2,4,6,7) require six head comparisons before the left sequence is exhausted. With constant-cost comparisons, access and copying, writing all m+n entries gives time complexity O(m+n) in Big O notation. Writing a separate output array needs m+n entry slots; the two positions require only constant additional storage.
The merge algorithm is useful whenever two already ordered collections must become one: it reads each input only forwards. This works with arrays and linked lists, without needing access to arbitrary middle positions. Choosing left on ties preserves each input's internal order and places equal left entries before equal right entries, which is the combination rule needed for stable sorting in merge sort.
The loop invariant behind algorithm correctness is that the emitted prefix is sorted, contains exactly the consumed entries, and every emitted key is at most every unconsumed key. Each sorted sequence has its smallest remaining key at its head, so the smaller of the two heads is safe to append. The invariant survives each removal; when one sequence ends, the other sorted remainder is safe to append in full. Each comparison removes an entry, so termination follows from the finite input lengths.

Binary search

Words: 428
Algorithm OurBigBook.com
Binary search finds a target x in a sorted array A by inspecting the middle of the remaining candidate range. If the middle entry is smaller than x, every entry to its left is also too small; if larger, every entry to its right is too large. One comparison therefore rules out many entries. Equal entries are allowed; this version returns any matching index, without promising the first occurrence.
Use indices starting at zero and inclusive endpoints L,R. Initially L=0, R=n−1, where n is the array length. While L≤R, choose
m=L+⌊2R−L​⌋.
(65)
The brackets denote the floor function. Compare Am​ with x: return m on equality; set L=m+1 if Am​<x; otherwise set R=m−1. If L>R, report absence. The updates exclude the already inspected middle entry. This also handles an empty array, whose initial endpoints are 0,−1. Sedgewick and Wayne specify a sorted array as input and return a matching index or −1 for absence.[ref]
For a fully worked example, take the sorted array
A=(2,5,8,12,16,23,38,56,72,91,104,130,160,205,260).
(66)
Search for x=23:
StepCandidate indicesMiddle index and valueConsequence
10…14m=7, A7​=5623<56: retain 0…6.
20…6m=3, A3​=1223>12: retain 4…6.
34…6m=5, A5​=23Return index 5.
For x=24, the first two steps agree. Next 24>23 retains only index 6; inspecting A6​=38 sets R=5. Now L=6>5=R, so the answer is "absent" after four comparisons.
The loop invariant is: the array stays sorted, 0≤L≤R+1≤n, and every index containing x lies between L and R. It holds initially. The sorted array property justifies each exclusion. Returning on equality gives a match; an empty candidate range implies absence. Crucially, this loop invariant allows x to be absent from the beginning.
For a nonempty range of size s=R−L+1, an unsuccessful comparison leaves at most ⌊s/2⌋ candidates. Thus sizes satisfy sk​≤⌊n/2k⌋ after k unsuccessful comparisons. This proves termination and, for n≥1, at most ⌊log2​n⌋+1 middle-entry comparisons. The final singleton still needs inspection: n=1 requires one comparison, not zero. For n=15, the bound is four. This is the halving argument behind logarithmic time complexity.[ref]
A decision tree with q binary tests has at most 2q leaves. Distinguishing n possible matching positions therefore requires q≥⌈log2​n⌉. This lower bound counts binary tests, whereas the bound above counts three-way comparisons.

Karatsuba multiplication

Words: 1k Articles: 7
Algorithm OurBigBook.com
Karatsuba multiplication is a divide-and-conquer algorithm for multiplication of integers. Splitting each operand into two blocks seems to require four smaller products; the Karatsuba three-product identity recovers the two cross terms together from just three products. Repeating that saving through recursion changes the time complexity from quadratic to O(nlog2​3), where n counts digits in a fixed positional notation. The exponent is about 1.585: the benefit comes from the algorithm, even though each splitting step needs more addition and subtraction.
The Karatsuba worked multiplication below computes 1234⋅5678=7,006,652 using 12⋅56, 34⋅78, and 46⋅134. The last operand already shows why “half-size” needs care: Karatsuba carry handling and Karatsuba recursion termination account for the extra digit. Karatsuba digit-operation cost states the operation model; Karatsuba practical crossover explains why the asymptotic saving alone does not select a useful threshold.
The original 1962 paper presents a binary numeral system automaton construction: its Theorem 2 and proof reduce multiplication to taking squares of numbers, then reduce a larger square of a number to three smaller squares of numbers. Its footnote explicitly addresses the extra digit in a sum of halves. The sequential time complexity analysis below uses a different operation model from that paper's automaton size and depth bounds, including its Boolean circuit realization without feedback.[ref]

Karatsuba operand splitting (x=aBm+b,y=cBm+d)

Words: 140
Karatsuba multiplication OurBigBook.com
Fix an integer base B≥2. Let x,y≥0 have at most n digits in positional notation, treating zero as one digit. For n>1, set m=⌈n/2⌉ using the ceiling function, and q=Bm. Euclidean division gives
a=⌊x/q⌋,b=x−aq,c=⌊y/q⌋,d=y−cq,
(67)
where 0≤b,d<q and 0≤a,c<Bn−m. The floor function selects the high block; the remainder selects the low block. Both operands must use the same q, including when their actual digit lengths differ.
For odd n, the low block has m digit positions and the high block has n−m=m−1. Leading zero padding aligns a shorter operand without changing its integer value. Padding to a power-of-two length is optional: the split itself works for every n. If power-of-two padding is used, the padded length is less than twice the original length, so it changes only a constant factor in the asymptotic analysis.

Karatsuba three-product identity (xy=acB2m+((a+b)(c+d)−ac−bd)Bm+bd)

Karatsuba multiplication OurBigBook.com
Compute exactly three smaller products,
p2​=ac,p0​=bd,ps​=(a+b)(c+d).
(68)
The distributive property gives ps​=ac+ad+bc+bd, so the cross coefficient is h=ps​−p2​−p0​=ad+bc. Recombine by
xy=p2​q2+hq+p0​,q=Bm.
(69)
The saving is that ad and bc are never separately multiplied. Multiplying a digit block by q or q2 shifts its position in positional notation; it does not require another general integer multiplication. Addition of the shifted results still requires Karatsuba carry handling.

Karatsuba worked multiplication

Words: 101
Karatsuba multiplication OurBigBook.com
Use decimal expansion, B=10, n=4, m=2, and q=100. The Karatsuba operand splitting is 1234=12⋅100+34, 5678=56⋅100+78. The Karatsuba three-product identity gives
p2​p0​ps​hxy​=12⋅56=672,=34⋅78=2652,=(12+34)(56+78)=46⋅134=6164,=6164−672−2652=2840,=672⋅10000+2840⋅100+2652=7,006,652.​
(70)
The third product has a three-digit operand. A small-input base case can evaluate these three products directly, or a smaller threshold can continue recursion. Either choice preserves the identity; only the operation count changes.
The same Karatsuba operand splitting handles 123⋅45: choose n=3, m=2, and write 123=1⋅100+23, 45=0⋅100+45. Then p2​=0, p0​=1035, ps​=24⋅45=1080, and h=45, giving 4500+1035=5535. A zero high block and unequal lengths require no new algebraic rule.

Karatsuba carry handling

Words: 180
Karatsuba multiplication OurBigBook.com
The blocks in the Karatsuba three-product identity are integers, not single digits: p0​ can need 2m positions and h can exceed q−1. Concatenating the displayed blocks therefore fails. Accumulate their shifted values with ordinary addition, normalizing each digit position by Euclidean division: a coefficient v becomes the digit vmodB, with carry ⌊v/B⌋ passed to the next position. Subtraction likewise propagates borrows. Although h≥0 for these nonnegative integers, intermediate digitwise subtraction can still borrow.
In the four-digit Karatsuba worked multiplication, grouping by base q=100 gives unnormalized coefficients [672,2840,2652], written from high to low. Normalize from the right: 2652=26⋅100+52; 2840+26=2866=28⋅100+66; 672+28=700=7⋅100+0. The final groups are [7,00,66,52], yielding 7,006,652. The zero group must retain its two positions.
Since a,b,c,d<Bm, their sums are less than 2Bm≤Bm+1 and can need m+1 digits. Allocate that extra digit before the third recursive product; discarding it can change the answer. The GMP manual describes this sum growth and uses a difference-based form to avoid it.[ref]

Karatsuba recursion termination

Words: 153
Karatsuba multiplication OurBigBook.com
For the sum-based Karatsuba three-product identity, a safe fixed base-case threshold is three digits or more. Return zero directly if either operand is zero; at or below the threshold, use ordinary digit-by-digit multiplication. Otherwise split by the maximum current operand length and invoke Karatsuba multiplication on (a,c), (b,d), and (a+b,c+d).
Each recursive operand has at most ⌈n/2⌉+1 digits. This is strictly less than n for n≥4, proving termination. A rule stopping only at one digit does not supply this guarantee: in base two, 3=112​ splits into 1,1, whose sum is 2=102​, still two digits. An implementation must choose a sufficient threshold or explicitly handle such nonshrinking calls. Leading zero padding must not be repeatedly added in a way that defeats the decreasing size measure.
For signed integers, multiply absolute values with the same nonnegative procedure and restore the sign afterwards. This changes the representation bookkeeping, rather than the three-product identity.

Karatsuba multiplication OurBigBook.com
Count a fixed-base digit addition, subtraction, digit copy, or single-digit multiplication as constant cost. Base B stays fixed as n grows; an entire arbitrary-length integer multiplication is not one constant-cost step. With this model, splitting, sum formation, shifts and recombination require O(n) digit operations. Ordinary digit-by-digit multiplication forms n2 digit products for two n-position operands. The GMP base-case description uses this rectangular product arrangement.[ref]
The ideal equal-half recurrence relation is
T(n)=3T(n/2)+O(n).
(71)
For n=2k, level j has 3j calls of size n/2j. If each internal call incurs exactly α times its size in additional digit work, that level contributes αn(3/2)j. There are 3k=nlog2​3 leaves. The geometric series of internal work is
αn∑j=0k−1​(3/2)j=2α(3k−2k).
(72)
Thus fixed positive leaf cost plus this internal work grows on the order of nlog2​3. In Big O notation, T(n)=O(nlog2​3). Removing one of four products at every level matters much more than saving just one at the root.
The literal sum-based implementation instead admits the upper bound
T(n)≤3T(⌈n/2⌉+1)+Cn
(73)
for a nondecreasing worst-case cost envelope above a fixed base-case threshold. The extra digit does not change the exponent: since ⌈n/2⌉+1≤n/2+3/2, subtracting three from the size makes each child's adjusted size at most half its parent's. Stop this comparison at any fixed threshold greater than three; its recursion depth is log2​n+O(1) and the level-work sum is bounded by the same geometric series up to constant factors. Exact call counts can depend on carries, zero shortcuts and the threshold, so they need not equal the ideal 3j at each depth.

Karatsuba practical crossover

Words: 170
Karatsuba multiplication OurBigBook.com
Karatsuba digit-operation cost explains eventual scaling, while a practical base-case threshold depends on the costs of addition, subtraction, copying and function calls relative to small integer multiplication. Using M(n)=An2+Dn+E for a base-case cost, one Karatsuba level costs 3M(n/2)+Fn+G: the quadratic coefficient falls to 3A/4, but the linear contribution includes 3Dn/2+Fn. Small operands can therefore cost more despite the smaller exponent. This comparison and the effect of implementation improvements on the threshold are described in the GMP manual.[ref]
The plotted crossover belongs only to the stipulated constants in its caption; its ordinary-method curve counts digit products alone, while the Karatsuba curve includes the chosen internal overhead. Selecting a threshold for real software requires measuring the actual implementation on its intended machine. With base B=2w for a fixed machine digit width w, the same analysis counts machine digits; it does not establish a universal crossover in decimal digits, bits, or elapsed time.

An optimal quantum witness can be chosen with nonnegative amplitudes, since the witness acceptance operator is entrywise nonnegative. The quantum witness is generally a superposition, rather than a computational basis vector. The stoquastic acceptance floor explains the lower limit b≥1/2 for a nontrivial soundness promise.

Including table preparation and a final verification query gives
T(m)=m+O(mN−m​​)+1.
(75)
Choosing m≍N1/3 balances both terms and gives T(m)=O(N1/3). The Grover rotation angle rounding bound gives success tending to one. This is a query bound; it does not make reversible table lookup free in a gate or physical-memory cost model.
